The candidate CUB-1800-2025 is deliberately modeled as one continuous polity from 1800-2025 precisely because Cuba's island territory did not change despite political transitions (Spanish colony to 1898, US occupation 1899-1902, Republic from 1902, full sovereignty 1934) -- i.e. the database's own periodization treats these as non-territorial (sovereignty/regime) changes, not scope changes, so the source and candidate agree on the same constant reporting territory throughout. The magnitudes are plausible for the whole island: sugar (median ~1.1M tonnes, Cuba was historically the world's largest cane sugar exporter), cattle (~4.3M head), coffee, and other staples are consistent with an island-wide agricultural economy of Cuba's size, showing no discontinuity that would suggest a scope change at 1898/1902/1934. The one geographic wrinkle -- the Isle of Pines (Isla de la Juventud, ~3,056 km2, ~2.8% of total area) had disputed sovereignty status 1898-1934 before formal cession to Cuba by treaty -- is a minor sliver that does not materially alter the territory match and is not flagged as a distinct reporting unit in Mitchell or elsewhere.

The assertion routes IIA "madagascar" agricultural-area/production rows for 1911-1945 to MDG-1882-2025, the only Madagascar polity in the database (single row spanning 1882-2025, wiki_status draft, so its claims are an unreviewed prior agent's hypothesis). The wiki's own sub-chain notes an unspecified "French colony (expanded)" period from 1912-1946 nested inside this row. External research confirms what that expansion was: the Comoro Islands were administratively attached to the French colonial government of Madagascar from 1912 until 1946/47, when they were re-separated as their own overseas territory following WWII. This means for most of the observed span (1912-1945, i.e. all but the first year), "Madagascar" as an administrative/reporting unit could have included the Comoros, whereas the candidate's polygon (CShapes 2.0, feature_year 1960, post-independence Madagascar) is the main island only. However, the Comoros (~2,236 km2) are negligible against Madagascar's ~587,000 km2, so even if IIA folded Comoro output into the Madagascar label the magnitude effect on the staple series (coffee ~66,000 ha, tobacco ~5,500 ha, beans ~29,500 ha) would be minor, and there is no evidence in the sampled items or magnitudes of a discontinuity at 1912 or 1946 that would indicate a scope jump. Since MDG-1882-2025 is the only existing Madagascar polity and the reporting territory did undergo a real (if minor) administrative change mid-span, this is a confirm at best_available rather than verified_equal.
verdict.wiki_note: The vague "French colony (expanded)" label for the 1912-1946 sub-period in the sub-chain refers to the Comoro Islands, which were administratively attached to the government of Madagascar from 1912 until 1946/47 (re-separated as their own overseas territory after WWII). This means the observed IIA span (1911-1945) is almost entirely within a period when "Madagascar" as an administrative unit could have included Comoro production, though Comoros' small size (~2,236 km2 vs ~587,000 km2) makes the magnitude effect on agricultural series minor.

verdict.basis: The observed span (1897-1960) falls entirely within the pre-1974 period during which Cyprus was a single British colonial administration over the whole island (~9,251 km2), with no internal partition, cession, or border change -- the only known territorial rupture (the 1974 Turkish occupation creating the TRNC-controlled north) occurs after the assertion's span ends in 1960, so it does not affect this observation. Independence in 1960 changed sovereignty, not territory. Mitchell's 'cyprus' crop series (wheat median 68,000t, barley 49,000t, wine 14,850t, citrus 28,000t, potatoes 49,000t) are magnitudes plausible for whole-island Mediterranean agricultural production on a 9,251 km2 island and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change. The wiki page (draft status, 3 source citations to biger-1995) documents the island's stable boundaries 1879-1974 and explicitly separates the post-1974 partition issue, which is corroborated by well-established general history (British Cyprus 1878-1960 was administered as the whole island) independent of the draft page itself.

The candidate IDN-1949-1963 covers independent Indonesia from the Dec 1949 transfer of sovereignty until the 1963 transfer of western New Guinea, explicitly EXCLUDING West New Guinea (retained by the Netherlands as a separate territory, tracked as its own polity NNG-1949-1963). The observed assertion span (1949-1960) lies entirely inside this period, and West New Guinea's transfer (1963) falls after the observed span ends, so no territorial change occurs within the observed years — the reporting territory is constant. West New Guinea was administered as a wholly separate Dutch colony throughout 1949-1962 (distinct administration, population, statistical apparatus), a fact independently corroborated by general historical literature (West New Guinea dispute), not merely asserted by the draft wiki page. Mitchell's country-level agricultural series for "Indonesia" in this era would reflect Indonesian government/FAO reporting for the independent republic, not the separately-administered Dutch colony. Staple magnitudes (rice paddy median 7.285M ha, cassava 1.456M ha, maize 2.232M ha) are entirely consistent with Indonesia proper's known agricultural scale (Java/Sumatra/etc.) and implausible as including West New Guinea, whose agricultural output was negligible by comparison — supporting continuity rather than a scope change. Neighbor segments (IDN-1800-1945, IDN-1945-1949) show a continuous national reporting chain with no indication of a split-label problem.

review.basis: Numbers first: median rice paddy area 7,285,000 ha, maize 2,232,000 ha, cassava 1,456,000 ha over 1949-1960. Indonesia's national rice harvested area was ~5.9 M ha in 1950 rising to ~7.3 M ha by 1960-61 (FAOSTAT's first year, 1961, is ~7.3 M ha), so a median of 7.29 M ha over the span is exactly national scale. The decisive test is the sub-territory fold-up direction: Java and Madura carried only slightly over half of Indonesian lowland rice area in this era (~3.6-4 M ha), and our own DB carries an explicit Java-and-Madura subnational row (IDN-JVM-1949-1951, 132,000 km2) that this label could have been a fold-up of — the magnitudes are roughly double a Java-only basis, so the label is the whole country, not a component. Cassava and maize are likewise at all-Indonesia, not Java-only, levels. Upward scope inflation is also excluded: there is no larger union or empire Indonesia could belong to in these years, and the only territorial question is western New Guinea, which the Netherlands administered separately until 1963 (NNG-1949-1963, 410,361 km2) and which was agriculturally negligible and not covered by Mitchell's Indonesia tables; the candidate row is defined precisely as Dutch East Indies minus western New Guinea, so it matches. No entrepot risk (these are domestic area/production series for staples Indonesia manifestly grows). Territory was constant across the entire observed span 1949-1960: the RUSI-to-unitary change of 1950 moved no borders, and the West Irian transfer (1963) falls after the observed data end and after the candidate's own end year, so a single polity does equal the reporting territory throughout. Boundary vintage is not an issue for a contemporaneously compiled Mitchell series. One caveat that belongs to the neighbouring segment, not this assertion: Mitchell's pre-independence Netherlands Indies crop series are frequently footnoted "Java and Madura only", so a step up at the 1949 boundary against IDN-1800-1945 would be a reporting-basis artefact rather than a territorial change, and should not be read as evidence against this routing. The wiki page is a draft; I used its territorial claim (Indonesia minus western New Guinea, 1,466,882 km2 vs 1,877,243 km2) only after independently confirming the West New Guinea chronology, and my verdict rests on the magnitudes.

verdict.basis: Mitchell's 'Chile' series (wine, beer, meat, milk, fish, livestock) for 1902-1960 reports on Chile's national territory, matching candidate CHL-1902-2025. The reviewed wiki page (5 source citations) documents Chile's boundaries as essentially settled after the War of the Pacific gains (1883-1884) but notes the final Chile-Peru boundary delimitation treaty of 3 June 1929 — a mid-span border adjustment (Tacna-Arica settlement) falling inside the 1902-1960 observed span. Because the reporting territory's exact extent shifted (however marginally) within the span rather than being constant throughout, confirm_kind is best_available rather than verified_equal. Staple magnitudes (e.g. wine ~108,000 t, meat ~158,500 t, milk ~598,000 t) are plausible for a mid-sized national economy of Chile's scale and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change at our period boundaries. The neighbor segment (1900-1901 -> CHL-1899-1902) shows smooth continuity into this polity.

The assertion covers France 1850-1870 (21 years, 265 rows of metropolitan agricultural series: wheat, barley, oats, potatoes, rye, flax, etc.), routed to FRA-1800-1871 (France with Alsace-Lorraine, 1800-1871). The candidate's own draft wiki page documents that this period is NOT territorially constant: it explicitly flags the March 1860 Treaty of Turin annexation of Nice and Savoy (+8,261 km², ~1.5% of metropolitan France) as occurring mid-span, with the polygon (CShapes 1816 vintage) understating true extent for 1860-1871 by that amount, while correctly including Alsace-Lorraine throughout (not ceded until 1871, after the observed span ends). Since the reporting territory grew mid-span via a real annexation, no single constant-territory candidate can equal it exactly across the whole 1850-1870 window, even though the wiki assesses the mismatch as minor and low-priority for a separate split. The staple magnitudes (wheat median 6.73M ha, oats 3.1M ha, potatoes 2.98M ha) are consistent with historical metropolitan French agricultural area in this era, supporting that this is genuine metropolitan France reporting (not a union/empire or Algeria-inclusive scope, and not an entrepot/re-export artifact). The neighbor_segments show continuation to FRA-1871-1919 for 1871-1918, consistent with the documented 1871 Alsace-Lorraine split being the intended discontinuity. No existing granular polity captures the pre-1860 vs 1860-1871 Nice/Savoy distinction, so best_available is the correct (not verified_equal) confirm.

Mexico's territory was stable from 1854 (post-Gadsden Purchase) through 2025, with only a sub-threshold 1963/1967 Chamizal adjustment — well after the observed span. The FAO 1952 "Mexico" label for 1937-1951 falls entirely within this stable-border period, so the reporting territory equals the candidate polity's territory for the whole span and did not change mid-span. The apparently low population magnitude (median 3,684k) is explained by the already-established source_convention: the item code mixes five population indicators (total, agricultural, agricultural-occupied, male/female splits); 3,684k is plausible as the agricultural-occupied (economically active in agriculture) indicator, not evidence of a territorial mismatch, consistent with the prior verification's findings for other countries in this same source. No entrepot, union, or sub-territory fold-up issue applies to "Mexico" as a national label.

The candidate ESP-1800-2025 tracks metropolitan Spain's borders as unchanged since 1815 (Congress of Vienna), and its wiki page documents multiple independent sources (CShapes 2.0, COW state-system, Biger 1995) all agreeing on a single static polygon with no European territorial change across the entire 1800-2025 span, including through 1937-1951. The observed assertion span (1937-1951) covers the Spanish Civil War (1936-39) and its aftermath — a major internal political rupture but not a change to Spain's international borders (no annexation, cession, or recognized partition; the war was a contest for control of the same fixed territory, resolved by 1939 with the same pre-war boundaries intact). The FAO 1952 yearbook, compiled retrospectively after the war's end, reports national totals for "Spain" as a single reporting unit; the staple magnitudes in the bundle (chick peas ~218k ha, groundnuts ~10k ha, tobacco ~13k ha, cotton lint ~12k ha, sugar ~182k tonnes) are plausible whole-country totals for a nation of Spain's size and agroclimatic profile, showing no sign of partial-territory reporting (e.g., Nationalist-zone-only or Republican-zone-only coverage) or of a large discontinuity that would flag a scope break. The wiki's own open question (oq-civil-war-1936) already flags the civil war as a documented caveat but correctly concludes it is not a territorial-change trigger under the WHEP polity-definition rule. Given metropolitan Spain's territory was genuinely constant through this span and the source's reporting unit matches, I confirm with verified_equal.

review.basis: I reconstructed the FAO 1952 yearbook's own country-table structure from the ingested layer B (consolidated_layer_b.parquet, source fao1952) rather than from the wiki. The publication lists every Spanish dependency under its OWN label — "Spanish Morocco"/"Spanish Moroccan Prot" (55 rows: cattle 254-279k head, goats 871-1,028k, rye, chickpeas), "Sp Morocco and possessions in North Africa" (land-use, total 4,587k ha), "Spanish Possessions in North Africa" (population total 128k in 1937, 142k in 1951 = Ceuta+Melilla), "Spanish Guinea" (coffee 4.3-7.2 kt), "Spanish Sahara", "Spanish West Africa". So the "Spain" label is NOT an empire aggregate and carries no combined reporting. Magnitudes under "Spain" are metropolitan-Spain-sized and internally coherent: population total 25,043k (1937) and 28,086k (1951), bracketing the 1940 (25.9M) and 1950 (28.0M) Spanish censuses; rye 489-514 kt, oats ~500-550 kt, rice paddy 280-302 kt on 57-63k ha, grapes 2.4 Mt on ~1.4M ha, oranges 712-1,086 kt, olives 0.9-1.9 Mt, chick peas 365-396k ha, tobacco 12-15k ha, cotton lint 29-55k ha — all peninsular-Spain scale, no fold-up of a province and no inflation toward an imperial total. Two scope refinements the label does carry: (a) the Canary Islands ARE inside "Spain" for most series — bananas 230 kt on 8k ha in 1949 can only be Canarian, an agronomic impossibility for the peninsula — yet the yearbook's tobacco table breaks them out as a separate "Spain Canary Islands" line (1.0k ha, 0.5-0.6 kt), so the parts are not treated uniformly; (b) Ceuta and Melilla, which the WHEP polity includes, sit outside "Spain" in this source, under "Spanish Possessions in North Africa". Both discrepancies are marginal (~0.5% of population, tens of km²), so the routing to ESP-1800-2025 is right, but they mean the reporting territory is not strictly identical to the polity's — hence best_available rather than verified_equal. Boundary vintage: Spain's metropolitan borders were unchanged 1937-1951 (Civil War and Franco regime brought no territorial change), so no split basis exists; the year-<NA> rows are the yearbook's prewar (1934-38) average column, same territory. I did not rely on the draft wiki page for any territorial claim; its assertions (borders stable since 1815, Ceuta/Melilla Spanish throughout) are independently correct, so it is neither suspect nor misleading here.
review.wiki_note: FAO Yearbook 1952 defines "Spain" as the peninsula plus the Balearics and the Canaries (bananas 230 kt on 8k ha in 1949 are Canarian — the peninsula cannot grow them), but EXCLUDES Ceuta and Melilla, which the yearbook reports separately as "Spanish Possessions in North Africa" (population 128k in 1937, 142k in 1951); Spanish Morocco, Spanish Guinea, Spanish Sahara and Spanish West Africa each have their own labels. One exception to the Canaries being folded in: the tobacco table breaks them out as "Spain Canary Islands" (1.0k ha), so Spain's tobacco line excludes them. Separate data-quality note: several of Spain's prewar-average (year-null) cells in the ingested layer B are extraction defects — oats 3,670 kt, rice paddy 3,293 kt and wine 41,926 kt are one to two orders of magnitude above the adjacent annual values.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes FAO1952 "Brazil" agricultural data (1937-1951) to BRA-1909-2025. The candidate's wiki page (draft status, but documenting CShapes-derived geometry with a clear cited claim) states Brazil's external borders were constant across 1909-1960 (identical CShapes geometry), meaning no territorial change occurred anywhere within the observed 1937-1951 span. There is no union/empire ambiguity (Brazil was never in a union), no combined-reporting risk, and no sub-territory fold-up concern since Brazil is a national-level source label reported at the country level. Staple magnitudes (240k tonnes meat, ~3.1M head horses/mules/asses, ~1.4M ha cottonseed, ~1.1M ha dry beans, 116k ha tobacco) are all plausible in scale for Brazil's ~8.47M km² national territory and population of the era, with no red flags of scope mismatch (e.g., no evidence these figures are too small for national coverage or too large for a sub-territory). The source_conventions entry for fao1952 (verified independently against consolidated_layer_b.parquet) documents that this source's country-level totals are reliable when using the correct indicator series, reinforcing that "Brazil" here is a straightforward national label. Since the territory was constant throughout the entire observed span and matches the candidate exactly, this qualifies as verified_equal rather than best_available.

The assertion routes FAO 1952's "French Morocco" label (1937-1951, 261 rows) to MAR-1911-1958. The wiki page (draft) contains a dated "Scope correction" section, independently corroborated against the polities CSV, establishing that this candidate is specifically the FRENCH protectorate zone (cshapes feature 600, 350,268 km2) as distinct from the separately-tracked SMO-1912-1956 (Spanish Morocco, feature 602, 52,792 km2). This is exactly the territory the FAO label "French Morocco" denotes -- not a fold-up of a sub-territory into a larger parent, but a like-for-like match. The observed span 1937-1951 lies entirely within the stable French-protectorate period (established 1912, ended 1956), with no annexation/cession/occupation event inside the span, so territory was constant throughout. Staple magnitudes (meat ~52k tonnes, horses/mules/asses ~183k head) are plausible for a territory this size; the population figure (median 1,334k) looks low for French Morocco's true ~6-7M population circa 1937-1951 but the bundle's own source_conventions entry already documents that this FAO population item code mixes five distinct indicators (total vs agricultural vs agricultural-occupied), so a low median is expected indicator-mixing noise, not evidence of a territorial mismatch -- this is a known, already-recorded caveat, not new information.

The assertion routes FAO 1952 yearbook data labeled "Austria" (1937-1951) to AUT-1919-2025. This span crosses the 1938 Anschluss (Austria annexed into Nazi Germany, no longer a sovereign COW entity until 1955) — a period the polity's own wiki flags as an unresolved open question (oq-anschluss-1938) about whether the row papers over a real political discontinuity. However, the land territory of Austria (the Saint-Germain 1919 borders) never physically changed across this span, and the reported staple magnitudes (meat ~100k tonnes, grapes ~80k ha, dry beans ~2k ha) are consistent with Austria's own modest ~83,879 km² scale across the full 1937-1951 window, not with a merged Greater-Germany reporting basis (which would show a large step up in 1938 and back down in 1945/1951 as German totals absorbed or released Austrian output). This corroborates the wiki's existing 2026-07-24 verification note (from a different source, "juan") that found the same territorial stability 1919-1960 across the Anschluss years for crop-area data — i.e. two independent sources both show FAO/juan reporting conventions kept "Austria" on its constant First-Republic/modern territorial basis regardless of the sovereignty interruption. Since a real annexation event (1938-1945) plus occupation (1945-1955) occurred mid-span, per the routing rule this cannot be verified_equal even though the territory itself is corroborated as unchanged and matched; it is best_available, since sovereignty (not land extent) shifted mid-span and the row itself conflates political periods the wiki flags as unresolved.
verdict.wiki_note: FAO 1952 yearbook staple magnitudes (meat ~100k tonnes, grapes ~80k ha, dry beans ~2k ha, poultry ~116k heads) for "Austria" 1937-1951 show no step at 1938 or 1945/1951 and stay consistent with Austria's own ~83,879 km² scale — a second, independent source corroborating the existing 2026-07-24 verification note (from the "juan" source) that Austria-labeled data was reported on its constant First-Republic/modern territorial basis throughout the 1938-1955 Anschluss/occupation period, not folded into Greater-German totals. This does not resolve oq-anschluss-1938 (the sovereignty-gap row-structure question) but does answer, for this source, whether its reporting territory shifted — it did not.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes IIA "israel"-labeled agricultural production data (1922-1945, iso_in_data=isr) to PAL-1920-1948 (British Mandate Palestine). The wiki page (draft status, but citing biger-1995 with 8 citations) documents that the Mandate territory was fixed from 1922 (after Transjordan's separation) through 1948 — i.e. the observed span 1922-1945 falls entirely within the post-1922, pre-1948 stable-boundary period, with no annexations/cessions in between. The staple magnitudes (olives ~45,800t, sesame ~6,200t, grapes ~18,000t, tobacco ~2,173ha) are plausible smallholder Mediterranean-agriculture volumes consistent with Mandate Palestine's known agrarian profile, not a larger or smaller reporting unit. iso_in_data="isr" reflects a retroactive/backfilled ISO label common in IIA/FAO historical series for the pre-1948 territory, but the actual reporting geography is the Mandate, matching the candidate. The wiki's own open question (oq-pal-1922-transjordan-separation) already flags the polygon-vintage nuance, so nothing new to add there.

review.basis: Territory first: in 1922-1945 there was no state of Israel; the land carrying ISO "isr" in this dataset was the British Mandate for Palestine. The label "israel"/iso "isr" is therefore a modern ISO3 relabel applied to what the IIA yearbooks tabulated as "Palestine", compiled from the Palestine Government's agricultural statistics — i.e. the territory west of the Jordan, Transjordan having been detached by the September 1922 memorandum before the mandate came into force in 1923. Scope checks: not a union/empire fold-up (Transjordan reported separately and is a separate polity chain, JOR-1923-1946); not a sub-territory fold-up (the label is the whole administrative reporting unit, not a district or the Jewish sector alone); no combined reporting; no entrepot risk in these commodities. Magnitudes corroborate Mandate Palestine rather than any narrower or broader unit: olives median 45.8 kt (alternate-bearing Palestinian olive crop ran in the tens of kt), sesame 6.2 kt, grapes 18 kt, tobacco 2,173 ha — all consistent with a ~26,000 km2 territory whose Arab-sector orchards dominated these crops, and far too large for the Jewish-settlement sector alone, far too small for Palestine-plus-Transjordan-plus-neighbours. I inspected data/geodata/polities_polygons.gpkg directly: PAL-1920-1948 measures 27,046 km2 (Mollweide) with an eastern bound at the Jordan/Dead Sea, i.e. the polygon is the post-1922 west-of-Jordan mandate and does NOT include Transjordan, so the assigned polygon matches the source's reporting territory. Why best_available and not verified_equal: the span opens in 1922, the very year of the Transjordan detachment, and the northern (Paulet-Newcombe) boundary was only settled in 1923, so the reporting territory was not strictly constant across the whole observed span even though it was effectively fixed from 1923 to 1945. No better-fitting existing polity exists and no split is warranted; the routing is correct.
review.wiki_note: Answers open question oq-pal-1922-transjordan-separation: the assigned CShapes 2.0 polygon (feature 665, vintage 1920) measures 27,046 km2 in equal-area projection with its eastern limit at the Jordan River / Dead Sea, so it EXCLUDES Transjordan and already represents the post-1922 mandate despite its 1920 feature year (compare ISR-1948-1967 at 20,783 km2). Also worth recording: pre-1948 data for this territory arrives in this pipeline under the modern label "israel"/iso "isr", which is an ISO3 relabel of the IIA's "Palestine" tables, not a claim about Israeli borders.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes FAO1952 "New Zealand" agricultural/livestock data (1937-1951) to NZL-1840-2025. New Zealand is a straightforward national reporting unit with no union/empire ambiguity (unlike Sweden-Norway, Austria-Hungary, etc.) and no plausible combined-reporting risk. The candidate's wiki page (draft status, but with 11 source citations and specific CShapes/Biger sourcing) documents that NZ's core territory (~268,122 km2, North/South/Stewart Islands) was stable from the 1860s through the present, with the only caveat being administered Pacific dependencies (Cook Islands, Niue, Western Samoa, Tokelau, ~1.25% of mainland area) that are NOT included in the CShapes polygon and were NOT part of FAO's national production/livestock statistics for New Zealand proper (Cook Islands trade was tracked separately/bilaterally per the wiki's own documented IIA footnote analysis). The staple_magnitudes (meat 218k tonnes, poultry 320k, other meat 4k) are plausible for NZ's known role as a major meat/dairy exporter in this era and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change across 1937-1951. The population median (147k) is flagged by an already-resolved source_convention note as an artifact of FAO1952's item-code mixing five distinct population indicators (total/agricultural/agricultural-occupied + splits) -- not a territorial signal -- so it does not undermine the match. The observed span (1937-1951) sits entirely within a period the wiki documents as territorially stable for mainland NZ, with no annexation/cession/occupation events. This is a clean, low-ambiguity national match.

New Zealand's mainland territory (~268,122 sq km, no land boundaries) was stable throughout 1909-1945: dominion status was attained in 1907 with no accompanying territorial change (CShapes area identical before/after the 1907-09-01 split), and no annexation or cession of the main islands (North, South, Stewart) occurred within this window. NZ-administered Pacific territories (Cook Islands, Niue, Western Samoa mandate from 1920, Tokelau) are excluded from the mainland polygon but total only ~1.25% of area and are not the source of mainland agricultural production data. The IIA yearbook items sampled (butter, cheese, eggs, flax fibre and tow, grapes; staple magnitudes for hops ~278 ha, rye ~200 t, tobacco ~1,000 ha, wine ~120 ha) are all plausible mainland-NZ agricultural products and scales, consistent with a single national reporting unit under the "New Zealand" label with no entrepot, combined-reporting, or sub-territory-foldup anomaly. Unlike Sweden-Norway or Austria-Hungary, no union/empire ambiguity applies to New Zealand in this period, so the label unambiguously denotes the New Zealand polity itself for the whole 1909-1945 span.

The assertion covers FAO1952's 'Algeria' label for 1937-1951, entirely within the candidate DZA-1919-1962's stable span (French colonial Algeria, 1919-1962, no territorial change per CShapes/biger-1995 -- next border shift is independence in 1962, well after the observed span). The source_conventions entry already resolved the FAO1952-series pitfalls (population indicator-mixing, extraction defects) for this dataset generally, and the items here (broad beans, camels, cattle, meat, phosphate rock) are ordinary agro-pastoral/mining output entirely plausible for colonial Algeria's own territory -- no entrepot/re-export signature and no sign this is a transit label for goods produced elsewhere. There is no combined-reporting risk: FAO reports 'Algeria' as its own line distinct from metropolitan France, matching the standard convention that French Algeria, though administratively integrated into France post-1848, was statistically enumerated separately in international series. No boundary-vintage concern arises since the whole 1937-1951 observed window falls inside the single 1919-1962 CShapes polygon period with no annexation/cession events in between. The wiki page (draft status, thin at 1904 bytes) does not itself verify the reporting territory in detail, but corroborates the stable colonial-Algeria territorial frame (predecessor/successor chain, CShapes area) used to reach this conclusion.

The assertion routes Mitchell's "Fiji" agricultural series (sugar cane, rice paddy; 254 rows, 1879-1960) to FJI-1800-2025 by ISO match. The wiki page (draft status, but with 16 source citations, not a bare CSV stub) makes a well-corroborated case that Fiji's territory was constant across 1800-2025: it is a ~332-island archipelago "with no land boundaries" (Biger 1995), so no treaty could move a frontier, and no boundary event is recorded anywhere in the source set. The only two sovereignty events in Fiji's history — 1874 Deed of Cession (British annexation) and 1970 independence — both fall OUTSIDE the observed span (1879-1960), so the reporting territory is not merely comparable but literally unchanged for the entire span being verified: the same islands under the same colonial administration throughout. The one caveat raised (Rotuma, ~47 km², 0.25% of area, sometimes separately administered) is explicitly assessed as immaterial to production magnitudes and is a labeling curiosity, not a territorial discrepancy. Staple magnitudes (sugar cane ~23,000 t median, rice paddy ~10,000 ha median) are plausible in scale for colonial Fiji's real sugar/rice sectors, not the impossible-for-geography pattern that would flag entrepot re-export. GADM polygon area (18,649 km²) and Biger's stated area (18,325 km²) agree to 1.8%, giving independent corroboration of the territory's size. No sub-territory fold-up risk (Fiji is not a component of some larger reporting unit) and no combined-reporting risk (no other territory plausibly folded into a Mitchell "Fiji" line). Given the span sits wholly within one unbroken colonial-territory period with no border-changing event before, during, or shortly after it, confirm/verified_equal is warranted despite the wiki's draft status, because the corroboration (Biger's no-land-boundary claim, absence of any boundary event, area cross-check) is independent of the page's own assertions.

review.basis: Numbers first: I pulled every Mitchell "fiji" row from state/matched_rows.parquet. Cane area rises smoothly 1,000 ha (1879) to 20,000 ha (1913) to 35,000 ha (1960); the tonnes series rises 1,000 to 100,000 to 287,000 (1959) with a sharp 1960 fall to 149,000 and dips in 1918-19, 1922-24 and 1942-44. Two things follow. (a) Scale: 35,000 ha of cane is ~1.9% of the archipelago's ~1.86 M ha land area (polygon 18,649 km2, Biger 18,325 km2) - exactly the order of magnitude for the whole Colony of Fiji's Viti Levu/Vanua Levu sugar belt, far too large for a single district or island, and not a fold-up of a component of a larger parent (the label is the colony itself; Fiji has no parent federation in this source). The 1959 level of ~287 kt matches the independently known fact that Fiji's sugar output reached roughly 0.3 Mt around 1960, and the 1960 collapse matches the 1960 cane-growers' strike - the series tracks Fiji's own history, not a wider reporting unit. (b) Continuity: no step anywhere in 1879-1960 that would betray a scope change, and no neighbor_segments to reconcile since WHEP carries Fiji as one undivided row. Failure families cleared: no union/empire scope (self-contained Crown Colony 1874-1970, no land boundary, nothing to aggregate or disaggregate); no boundary-vintage problem (an archipelago with no land frontier); no combined reporting; no entrepot risk (Fiji genuinely grew the cane and rice, and the rice series at ~15-30 kt on 10-15k ha is a sensible ~2 t/ha paddy yield). One real caveat forces best_available rather than verified_equal: Rotuma was annexed in 1881, inside the observed span, so the reporting territory was not literally constant end to end - at ~47 km2 (0.25%) it cannot move any series, and I could not settle whether colonial returns included it (the wiki's own open question oq-fji-rotuma-reporting-scope; Mitchell states no area for its label). Separately, a source-convention finding rather than a territory one: the item labelled "sugar cane" in tonnes is NOT cane tonnage - 149,000 t on 35,000 ha in 1960 is 4.3 t/ha, a raw-sugar yield, whereas cane would be 50-70 t/ha (~2 Mt). Indonesia's Mitchell rows show the same ~6 t/ha signature. Routing is unaffected. The wiki page (draft, 8.7 KB, 16 citations) is unusually solid for a draft and its territorial reasoning holds up independently via Biger's area and the no-land-boundary argument, but I did not need it to reach the verdict and do not rest on it.
review.wiki_note: Mitchell's "sugar cane" series for Fiji in tonnes measures raw/centrifugal SUGAR, not cane tonnage: 1960 gives 149,000 t on 35,000 ha (4.3 t/ha) and 1959 gives 287,000 t, whereas cane would run 50-70 t/ha (~2 Mt). The 1959 peak and the sharp 1960 drop correspond to Fiji's record crop and the 1960 cane-growers' strike, corroborating that the series is Fiji-wide sugar output. Rotuma (oq-fji-rotuma-reporting-scope) stays unsettled - Mitchell states no area for its Fiji label - but at 0.25% of land area it is below the noise in these series.

source_convention.convention: In Mitchell's International Historical Statistics agricultural tables, the 'sugar cane' series expressed in tonnes is raw/centrifugal sugar OUTPUT, not cane tonnage; the paired 'sugar cane' series in hectares is cane area. Treating the tonnes series as cane understates production by roughly an order of magnitude.
source_convention.evidence: Fiji 1960: 149,000 tonnes on 35,000 ha = 4.3 t/ha, and 1959: 287,000 t - raw-sugar yields; cane at 50-70 t/ha would imply ~2 Mt. Fiji's known sugar output reached ~0.3 Mt around 1960 with a sharp 1960 fall from the cane-growers' strike, matching the tonnes series. Indonesian Mitchell rows show the same ~6 t/ha (sugar) signature.

verdict.basis: Checked the FAO-1952 layer-B rows for country=='Netherlands' directly: the item_code r_fao_population_1952_10_18 carries a "population total" indicator with 8,598k (1937) and 10,264k (1951) people — matching the real historical population of metropolitan Netherlands, not a colonial subset. The Dutch East Indies-era colonies appear under clearly separate country labels in the same source ('Netherlands New Guinea', 'Netherlands West Indies'), confirming the 'Netherlands' label is metropolitan-only and not combined-reporting with colonies. The bundle's low "median 589" population figure is fully explained by the already-resolved source_convention (five population indicators sharing one item code; agricultural/agricultural-occupied subsets pull the naive median down) — not a new finding. The candidate NLD-1830-2025's wiki page (draft, 5120 bytes, 2 citations) documents that Dutch European borders have been stable since the 1839 Treaty of London and separately flags the 1940-1945 German-occupation gap in COW membership (oq-cow-code-na) — this is a genuine sovereignty interruption falling inside the observed 1937-1951 span. Per the routing instructions, an occupation mid-span disqualifies verified_equal even when land boundaries were physically unchanged, so despite territorial continuity this must be recorded as best_available rather than verified_equal.

The assertion's observed span (1938-1960) falls entirely within candidate BOL-1938-2025 (1938-2025), whose start date is anchored to the 1938 Chaco War peace treaty that fixed Bolivia's modern borders. The reviewed wiki page (6 source citations, no TODOs) documents this territorial history with specifics (area 1,098,587 km2, landlocked, Chaco War settlement) sourced to biger-1995. The neighbor segment shows 1910-1937 correctly routes to the predecessor BOL-1909-1938, confirming the 1938 period split aligns with the actual boundary change rather than being arbitrary. Staple magnitudes (potatoes ~113k t, wheat ~23k t, barley ~50k t, coffee ~4k t, rice paddy ~17.5k ha) are all plausible for Bolivia's own landlocked Andean/lowland agriculture at this population/area scale, with no signs of entrepot re-export or sub-territory fold-up. No annexation, cession, or occupation affected Bolivia's territory between 1938 and 1960, so the reporting territory stayed constant across the whole observed span.

The assertion routes 248 rows of Juan's Peru production/area data (1922-1941, rice, cotton, wheat, sugar cane, cottonseed oil, livestock) to candidate PER-1922-1942 by ISO match. This is a standard national-level agricultural dataset (crop areas in hectares, tonnage) fully consistent with mainland Peru's known agricultural geography — no entrepot or sub-territory fold-up signature (these are staple domestic crops, not goods implausible for Peru's climate/terrain). The candidate is COW ccode=135 (Peru), matching the neighbor segments PER-1884-1909 / PER-1909-1922 / PER-1922-1942 / PER-1942-2025, a clean sequential national-polity chain with no indication of scope change at these split points. The only territorial event in the span is the minor 1932-33 Leticia incident with Colombia (a small trapezium of Amazonian territory Peru had already ceded in principle in 1922 and briefly occupied), which is too small relative to Peru's total area to constitute a material change in reporting territory for national agricultural statistics. The 1942 end-of-row event (Rio Protocol/Ecuador border) is a border settlement, not a change during the observed span itself. The wiki page is a draft, thin CSV-derived stub (1812 bytes, 1 source citation) that documents only the polygon source and predecessor/successor chain — it offers no independent territorial verification and is not being relied upon as evidence; the confirm rests instead on the plausibility of the magnitudes for mainland Peru and the coherence of the ISO/COW national-polity chain.

The candidate COL-1922-2025 is post-Panama-secession Colombia (Panama separated 3 Nov 1903), with stable modern borders (area ~1,138,908 km2 per Biger-1995) that did not change across the observed 1922-1960 span. Neighbor segments confirm the 1903 secession is already handled by an earlier polity split (COL-1903-1922 covers 1903-1921), so the 1922-onward candidate begins after that territorial change and remains constant through 1960 -- no annexation, cession, or occupation affecting Colombia in this window. Staple magnitudes (cacao ~11,000t, sugar ~70,000t, cotton seed ~11,000t) are consistent in scale with a mid-sized South American agricultural economy of Colombia's size, with no discontinuities suggesting a scope change. The wiki page is 'reviewed' status with 6 source citations (COW, Biger-1995) documenting the territorial history accurately; no sub-territory fold-up, union/empire ambiguity, combined reporting, or entrepot concerns apply to a national-level 'Colombia' label with ISO code COL.

review.basis: I inspected the source rows themselves in the consolidated layer B extract (/home/usuario/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.csv, source=mitchell, country='colombia', 269 rows 1901-1960). The Mitchell country list contains a single plain 'colombia' label with no Colombian sub-units (contrast 'china, manchuria province of', 'cape province', 'natal', which show the compilation does break out components where it means them), so there is no sub-territory fold-up and no combined-reporting risk: Colombia held no colonies and no union partner in 1922-1960, and Panama had already seceded in 1903, before the observed span. The commodity mix (cacao beans, centrifugal sugar, cotton seed/lint, cassava, sugar cane, beer of barley) is agronomically native to Colombia at exactly these magnitudes — cacao rising 4 kt (1922) to 15 kt (1951), raw sugar 30-40 kt in the late 1920s to ~70 kt median, beer ~266 kt (~2-3 million hl, right for mid-century Colombia) — so no entrepot/re-export signature. Boundary vintage: the cacao series runs perfectly smoothly across our 1903-1922 / 1922-2025 split (4,000 t in both 1921 and 1922, same table page_33_table_1), i.e. Mitchell reports one continuous national series and our 1922 period break is invisible to this source; the routing of the 1922-1960 tail to COL-1922-2025 is nonetheless correct. I withhold verified_equal only because the reporting territory did not stay constant across the span: the Salomón-Lozano Treaty (signed 24 March 1922, ratified by Peru Dec 1927, Peruvian withdrawal from Leticia 1930, confirmed by the 1934 Rio Protocol after the Leticia war) shifted roughly 100,000 km² of Caquetá-Putumayo/Leticia-trapezium territory into Colombian control after 1930, while the candidate's polygon is CShapes vintage 1922 — so a single polygon cannot equal the reporting territory for both halves of 1922-1960. The effect on these series is nil (Amazon rainforest, no measurable cacao/sugar/cotton output), which is why the routing is the best available rather than wrong.
review.wiki_note: The page's "Modern Colombia with stable borders" is imprecise for the early part of the row: under the Salomón-Lozano Treaty (signed 1922, ratified by Peru 1927) roughly 100,000 km² of the Caquetá-Putumayo strip including Leticia and the Amazon trapezium only passed to effective Colombian control in 1930, and was confirmed after the 1932-33 Leticia war by the 1934 Rio Protocol; the assigned polygon is CShapes vintage 1922, i.e. pre-transfer. Production impact on agricultural series is negligible (rainforest). Separately, the Mitchell extract reports 'cotton lint' for Colombia in hectares rather than tonnes (median 68,000 ha, n=14) — an item/unit mismatch worth checking in the ingest, not a territory issue.

verdict.basis: Assertion routes USDA/FAO-style "united states of america" agricultural data (almonds, lettuce, maize, apples, etc.) for 1959-1960 to USA-1959-2025. This is the modern 50-state USA beginning with Alaska (Jan 1959) and Hawaii (Aug 1959) statehood — a well-established, externally verifiable historical fact independent of the draft wiki page. The observed span (1959-1960) falls entirely within the post-statehood period, so there is no mid-span territorial change to worry about (the pre/post-Alaska-Hawaii split happens within 1959 itself per CShapes, but "United States of America" as a reporting label for USDA/FAO-style agricultural statistics has always meant the full federal territory as currently constituted, not a sub-national fragment). Staple magnitudes (maize ~72M ha, apples ~1.4M ha, lettuce ~926k ha) are squarely in the range of known US national agricultural output for that era, consistent with a national-level label, not a sub-territory or a broader union. No entrepot, no combined-reporting, no sub-territory fold-up applies (USA is the full sovereign reporting unit here, not a component). Territory has remained constant (~9.46-9.8M km2) from late 1959 through 2025 with no annexations/cessions, so confirm with verified_equal is appropriate. The wiki page (draft status) documents this history consistent with external knowledge, but I am not relying on it alone — the statehood dates and territorial stability are common historical knowledge, and the data magnitudes independently corroborate a national-US-scale reporting territory.

The assertion covers Peru 1947-1951 under the FAO 1952 yearbook's plain country label 'Peru', a standard national-agriculture reporting unit with no union, combined-reporting, or sub-territory fold-up risk (unlike cases such as Sweden-Norway or Yemen). The candidate PER-1942-2025 starts precisely at 1942, the year Peru's modern borders were fixed by the Rio Protocol ending the 1941-42 war with Ecuador, and the wiki page (status: reviewed, 4 source citations from Biger 1995 and COW) explicitly documents "stable borders post-Protocol of Rio de Janeiro" with a clean predecessor link to PER-1922-1942 for the pre-war territory. The observed span 1947-1951 sits comfortably inside 1942-2025 with no annexation, cession, or occupation affecting Peru in that window, and the neighbor_segments field confirms the adjacent 1929-1937 span was correctly routed to the prior polity PER-1922-1942, showing period splits are already aligned to the border change. Staple magnitudes (horses/mules/asses ~432k head, groundnuts ~2k ha) are plausible for a mid-20th-century Peru of this size and show no discontinuity suggesting a different reporting territory.

Assertion routes FAO 1952 "Belgium" (1937-1951, 244 rows across broad beans, butter, carcass weights, poultry, tobacco, phosphoric acid, population) to BEL-1831-2025. Belgium's metropolitan territory has been stable and unambiguous since the 1919 Eupen-Malmedy acquisition (well before this span) and through the WWII occupation (1940-1944), which changed administration/sovereignty exercise but not the formal reporting territory FAO would use for a 1952 yearbook compiling national series. There is no union/empire-scope ambiguity here (unlike Sweden-Norway or Austria-Hungary) — "Belgium" in a mid-20th-century FAO table means metropolitan Belgium, distinct from the Belgian Congo, and the commodity mix (broad beans, butter, cattle/sheep carcass weights, poultry, tobacco, phosphoric acid) is exactly metropolitan Belgian agriculture/industry, not colonial produce — no entrepot/re-export or sub-territory fold-up signal. Magnitudes are plausible for Belgium's size: meat 142k tonnes, tobacco 3k ha, phosphoric acid 160k tonnes (Belgium had a real chemical/phosphate-processing industry) all fit a small industrialized country. The population median of 520 (1000s) looks too low for Belgium's true ~8.5M population at first glance, but the bundle's own source_conventions entry (verified 2026-08-14) explains this item code conflates five population indicators (total, agricultural, agricultural-occupied, male/female splits) and that agricultural-occupied is often ~10-20% of total for industrialized economies (matches the convention's own examples, e.g. Germany 12.4%, USA 6.5%) — Belgium being highly industrialized/urbanized would plausibly show an even lower agricultural-occupied share, so ~520k as that indicator is consistent rather than a red flag. No annexation/cession/separation event touches Belgium's territory during 1937-1951 itself (Eupen-Malmedy was 1919, well before the span), so the reporting territory was constant across the whole observed span, supporting verified_equal rather than best_available.

Mitchell's Pakistan series (1949-1960) reports agricultural statistics for the country as reported prior to the 1971 secession of East Pakistan — i.e., united Pakistan (West + East Pakistan/Bengal combined). This is well-established historical fact independent of the wiki: Pakistan existed as a single sovereign state from 1947 (with a 1949 CShapes polygon break likely reflecting the Kashmir ceasefire line, not a territorial change to Pakistan itself) until the 1971 secession of East Pakistan as Bangladesh. The candidate PAK-1949-1971 spans exactly this united-Pakistan period, and the observed assertion span (1949-1960) sits entirely inside it with no annexation, cession, or split occurring during those years — the only territorial change (the 1971 split) occurs after the observed span ends. The staple magnitudes are plausible for combined West+East Pakistan: median rice paddy area of ~9.98M ha is consistent with East Pakistan/Bengal being a major historical rice region, far too large for West Pakistan alone (which is arid/irrigated wheat-cotton country), confirming the data reflects the full combined territory rather than a sub-component. Neighbor segments show continuity with predecessor PAK-1947-1949, consistent with Mitchell reporting a continuous "Pakistan" series across this internal CShapes boundary tweak. The wiki page (draft status) documents this territorial scope correctly and consistently with external knowledge of Pakistan's history, so it corroborates rather than being the sole basis.

review.basis: Territory first: from 14 Aug 1947 Pakistan was a two-winged state — West Pakistan (Sindh, Punjab, NWFP, Balochistan plus acceded princely states) and East Bengal/East Pakistan. Across 1949-1960 the outline was broadly stable but not literally constant: the acceded princely states (Bahawalpur, Khairpur, Balochistan States Union) were only merged into the One Unit of West Pakistan in 1955, Gwadar was purchased from Oman in September 1958 and added to Balochistan, and the Kashmir position (Azad Kashmir / Northern Areas behind the 1949 Karachi ceasefire line) is de facto administered but almost certainly outside the statistical reporting universe, while the CShapes 770/1949 polygon's treatment of it is undocumented. One polity therefore cannot be asserted to equal the reporting territory exactly for the whole span — hence best_available, not verified_equal. The data settles the real risk here, combined East+West scope: rice/paddy median 9,983,000 ha. West Pakistan's total cropped area in the 1950s was roughly 11 Mha with paddy only ~1.2-1.5 Mha (Indus agriculture is a wheat/cotton system); ~8.5 Mha of aman/aus/boro paddy in East Bengal accounts for the remainder. A 10 Mha paddy area is agronomically impossible for the western wing alone, so Mitchell's "pakistan" here is united Pakistan including East Pakistan — exactly the candidate's extent. Companion magnitudes fit a combined unit dominated by the west for dryland crops (barley 214k ha, maize 434k, millet 607k, sugar cane 230k). Neighbor segments (PAK-1937-1947 for 1945-46, PAK-1947-1949 for 1947-48) show the same label continuing across our splits with no scope step, so no boundary-vintage or sub-territory fold-up problem; the label is not a component of a larger parent (none exists) and no entrepot issue arises for field crops. I did not rely on the draft wiki page for the territorial claim; the magnitudes decided it, and the page merely corroborates the two-wing extent.
review.wiki_note: Double-count risk in the database, not in this routing: polities_database.csv also contains BGD-1947-1971 "East Pakistan (1947-1971)" (cshapes 771, predecessor PAK-1937-1947), which claims the eastern wing for exactly the years PAK-1949-1971 also claims it, and both list BGD-1971-2025 as successor. Mitchell's "pakistan" 1949-1960 series are united-Pakistan totals (paddy ~10.0 Mha, of which ~8.5 Mha is East Bengal), so anything routed to BGD-1947-1971 for those years double-counts against this series. Worth also recording that Gwadar was only acquired (from Oman) in 1958 and that Azad Kashmir / Northern Areas are almost certainly outside the reported statistical territory whatever the polygon covers.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes 243 rows of Mitchell data (1850-1960, iso "tto") to TTO-1800-2025, WHEP's single national-scope row for Trinidad and Tobago spanning the whole 1800-2025 period. The candidate's wiki page (draft status, but backed by 5 source citations to Biger 1995, an authoritative historical-boundaries gazetteer) documents that Trinidad was acquired by Britain in 1802 and Tobago was administratively combined with it in 1889, but this only changed governance, not territorial extent - both islands were British possessions throughout, so WHEP deliberately keeps one row for the whole span (this was reaffirmed in a 2026-08-17 decision reversing a planned 1886 split). I independently checked the raw Mitchell source file (Nextcloud outputs/mitchell_data.csv) and found the label "trinidad and tobago" is used continuously and retroactively even for years well before the 1889 union (e.g. 1799-1818 sugar data already carries the combined label with iso "tto"), confirming the source itself reports the two islands as one unit for the entire span, with no separate "tobago"-only series to worry about a fold-up/combined-reporting issue. Staple magnitudes (sugar ~58,000t, cacao ~24,000t, sugar cane ~24,000ha) are plausible for a small twin-island economy and show no discontinuity suggesting a territorial scope change. No annexation, cession, or separation affected these islands' extent during 1850-1960 (independence in 1962 is outside the observed span and, per the WHEP row design, didn't need a split anyway since it didn't change territory, only sovereignty within the same row's design). Territory is constant across the whole observed 1850-1960 span and equals the candidate's documented extent, so verified_equal is appropriate.

The assertion routes IIA's "Sri Lanka" label (1909-1945, 242 rows: cacao, coffee, cotton, rubber, tea, tobacco) to candidate LKA-1800-2025 ("Sri Lanka", 1800-2025, national). The candidate's draft wiki page argues the island's coastline boundary never moved: Ceylon became a British colony in 1815 and independent in 1948, but neither transition altered territory, since Sri Lanka is an island with no land boundaries (Biger 1995 foreword, p.8, cited). This reasoning is independently checkable and sound — political status changes (colony to independent state) do not by themselves imply a territorial change for an island whose only boundary is its coastline, and I found no historical partition, cession, or annexation affecting Ceylon/Sri Lanka in 1800-2025. During 1909-1945 (British Ceylon), IIA (International Institute of Agriculture) yearbooks reported the colony as a single administrative/statistical unit — there is no sub-territory fold-up risk (Ceylon was not itself a component of a larger reporting unit at this time, unlike e.g. Bohemia-in-Austria cases) and no entrepot risk (tea, rubber, cacao, coffee, cotton, tobacco are all bona fide Ceylon plantation crops, not transit goods). Staple magnitudes (tea median 185,192 ha; cacao 4,001 t; tobacco 5,700 ha; cotton lint 160 ha; coffee 260 ha) are plausible in scale for the whole island's known plantation economy of that era, not for some fractional sub-region, supporting that the label denotes the whole reporting territory the candidate polity covers. Given the span (1909-1945) sits entirely within a period of constant island territory under one administration, and no boundary change occurred at any point across the full observed span, this is a case where verified_equal is warranted rather than merely best_available.

Mitchell's "algeria" label for 1886-1901 sits entirely within candidate DZA-1886-1902's span (1886 to 24-Dec-1902), during which French Algeria's territory (the three northern départements) was administratively stable — the only boundary event in this era, the Sahara annexation, falls at the very end of 1902, after the observed data years (1886-1901) close. The draft wiki page (3 source citations to Biger 1995) documents this: three French departments from 1848, integrated with France 1881, Sahara annexed as separate military zone only in Dec 1902. Mitchell's reported items (wheat/barley/oats hectarage, wine, tobacco) are agricultural staples consistent with the Mediterranean-climate coastal/tell departments and implausible for the Saharan south regardless of political boundary, so magnitudes cannot by themselves distinguish "three departments" from "three departments + Sahara" — but since the political territory itself did not change until after the span ends, this is moot: the reporting territory is the constant, unchanging French Algeria of the departments for the entire 1886-1901 window. Neighbor segments (pre-1886 -> DZA-1831-1886, post-1902 -> DZA-1902-1919) are consistent with our period splits bracketing this territorially stable middle segment. No sub-territory fold-up, entrepot, or union-scope issue applies (Algeria was administratively part of metropolitan France by this era but Mitchell reports it as its own line, matching the candidate's own separate national/colonial entry, not a French-metropolitan aggregate).

The candidate F51-1938-1945 is Czechoslovakia's 1938-1945 row (Munich→Vienna Award→German occupation→liberation), draft wiki, area falling 140,398→116,616→100,822 km² across the span; its own "Contradictions" section already documents that the sibling 'juan'/Mitchell-FAO series ignores this wartime shrinkage entirely (constant reporting). For IIA specifically, pipelines/polity-autoimprove/state/iia_label_provenance.csv classifies the raw label 'czechoslovakia' as whole_with_sub_siblings, sharing our normalized 'czech republic' bucket with the raw sub-label 'czechoslovakia: bohemia, moravia and silesia' (sub_of_sibling) - i.e. the pipeline's own harmonisation mapping already flags that a whole-country row and a ~1/3-scale component row collapse onto the same label, and per validate_iia_label_provenance.py's own description, when this happens 'one silently wins' per cell with no trace of which. I pulled the actual annual layer-B values (Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.csv, source=iia, country='czech republic', ha unit) for 1936-1945: rye area is ~967k-1,016k ha in 1936-1938 (whole-country scale), then collapses to 98k/78k/78k ha in 1939-1941 and 26k ha in 1943 (component/Protectorate scale, roughly a tenth), then jumps BACK to 861k ha (1942) and 915k ha (1944) before 802k ha in 1945. This is not a single boundary-vintage mismatch (constant wrong scale) like the juan finding - it is a year-by-year FLIP between whole-country and sub-component magnitudes within the same 1938-1944 span, with no clean contiguous break to hang a split_reroute on (1942 and 1944 revert to whole-country scale between years of component-scale reporting). No finer-grained Protectorate/Bohemia-Moravia polity exists in the DB to reroute the small years to. This is exactly the label-mixing defect the pipeline's own provenance file already names as a known hazard, now confirmed concretely for this key rather than merely theoretical - it makes any single verdict (confirm, even best_available) potentially misleading for roughly half the observed years, so I am flagging it as genuinely uncertain rather than forcing a confirm.
verdict.wiki_note: New finding, not in the page: for the IIA source specifically (distinct from the already-documented 'juan' contradiction), annual rye-area values under label 'czech republic' 1936-1945 (ha, from layer_b) alternate between whole-Czechoslovakia scale (~967k-1,016k in 1936-1938, ~861k-915k in 1942/1944, 802k in 1945) and roughly a tenth of that (98k/78k/78k/26k in 1939-1941/1943) - matching pipelines/polity-autoimprove/state/iia_label_provenance.csv's classification of 'czechoslovakia' (whole) and 'czechoslovakia: bohemia, moravia and silesia' (sub-component) as sharing one normalized label ('whole_with_sub_siblings' / 'sub_of_sibling'). Unlike the juan case (constant wrong vintage throughout), this IIA series flips territorial scope year-by-year with no clean contiguous split point, so no single split_reroute is currently possible; a Protectorate-of-Bohemia-Moravia polity does not exist in the DB to route the small years to.

review.basis: I worked from the numbers first, pulling the raw rows out of ~/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.csv (source=='iia', country=='czech republic'). Levels for 1939-1945 are whole-Czechoslovakia scale, not Protectorate scale: oats 706k/799k/655k/636k/602k/572k ha for 1939-44 and 599k ha in 1945, rye ~0.8-1.0M ha. The Protectorate of Bohemia-Moravia was ~49,000 km2 with ~2.6M ha arable and roughly half to two-thirds of interwar Czechoslovak cereal area, so a ~700k ha oats figure cannot be Protectorate territory; equally decisive, there is NO step at either territorial break — 1938 (1,016k ha rye, 770k oats in the parallel series) to 1939, and 1944 (572k oats) to the restored state in 1945 (599k) and 1947 (590k) are smooth. A shrinkage to the Protectorate and back would have shown a ~40-60% trough. Cross-checking against source=='juan', country=='czechoslovakia' for the same years, the iia values are IDENTICAL number-for-number (oats 706/799/655/636/602/572/599; rye 1,016k in 1938, 861k in 1942, 915k in 1944), so this label rides the same constant-territory compilation the candidate's wiki page already documents for juan. Reporting territory is therefore constant pre-Munich Czechoslovakia (~140,000 km2), NOT the candidate's actual 1938-1945 extent (CShapes post-Vienna-Award polygon, 100,713 km2) and not the wartime Protectorate. No polity row in polities_database.csv carries a constant pre-Munich basis across 1938-1944 (F51-1918-1938 ends in 1938), and the label is not a sub-territory fold-up (its magnitudes are larger than the candidate, not smaller), so F51-1938-1945 remains the best available home for these rows and no split or reroute would improve them — but this is a boundary-vintage mismatch and must not be recorded as verified_equal. Note also that the bundle's staple_magnitudes for this assertion are unreliable: the iia extract for this label is corrupted (rye ha shown as 98,000/78,000/26,000 for 1939/1940/1943 where the same series reads 984,000/708,000/926,000 — dropped leading digits — and the rows labelled 'wheat' at 5,000-28,000 ha are two orders of magnitude below Czechoslovak wheat, ~850-900k ha, so that item label is misassigned). I did not let those corrupted cells drive the verdict.
review.wiki_note: The constant pre-Munich territorial basis this page already documents for the `juan` series also holds for `iia`: the iia rows under label "czech republic" for 1938-1945 are numerically IDENTICAL to juan's "czechoslovakia" rows (oats 706/799/655/636/602/572/599 thousand ha 1939-45; rye 1,016k ha 1938, 861k 1942, 915k 1944), so the contradiction is source-wide across both compilations, not juan-specific. Separately, the iia extract of this label is damaged: rye area for 1939/1940/1943 appears as 98,000/78,000/26,000 ha where the parallel series reads 984,000/708,000/926,000 (dropped leading digits), and the rows labelled "wheat" (5,000-28,000 ha) are ~2 orders of magnitude below actual Czechoslovak wheat area (~850-900k ha), i.e. that item label is misassigned. Downstream users should not take iia rye/wheat areas for this label at face value.

source_convention.convention: In `iia`, the label "czech republic" (a modern-name harmonization; no "slovakia" or "czechoslovakia" label exists in the iia extract) reports CONSTANT pre-Munich Czechoslovak territory (~140,000 km2) straight through 1938-1945, not the shrinking wartime state or the Protectorate of Bohemia-Moravia.
source_convention.evidence: iia values for 1939-45 are identical to juan's "czechoslovakia" series and show no discontinuity at either the 1938 Munich/Vienna-Award contraction or the 1945 restoration (oats ha: 770k 1938, 706k 1939, 572k 1944, 599k 1945, 590k 1947).

verdict.basis: The observed span (1860-1885) falls entirely within the window the candidate's own wiki page dates as territorially stable: French control over northern Algeria (Algiers, Oran, Constantine departments) was consolidated by 1847-1848 and the Sahara was not annexed until 1902, so no boundary event touches 655,282 km² Algeria between 1847 and 1886. The two in-span events the page documents (1845 Lalla Marnia treaty fixing the Morocco frontier, 1881 administrative integration with France) are non-territorial or merely confirm an existing line, not a scope change. The successor row DZA-1886-1902 shares the identical 655,282 km² polygon, confirming continuity right through and past the observed span; the area only jumps (to 2,442,683 km², +273%) at the 1902 Sahara annexation, well outside this assertion's range. Mitchell's reported staple magnitudes for the period (wheat ~683k t, barley ~806k t, cattle ~1.11M head) are plausible for a Mediterranean/High-Plateau agricultural and pastoral economy of this size and are not consistent with any desert-inclusive territory, corroborating the northern-Algeria-only reporting scope independently of the wiki's narrative. Because the whole observed span sits inside a single constant-territory regime that also equals the candidate's own dated extent, this is a verified_equal confirm rather than best_available.

Jamaica is an island British colony throughout 1909-1945 (independence not until 1962), with no land boundaries and thus no plausible territorial change in this span. The wiki page (draft status) already documents specific corroboration for this exact source: IIA yearbooks report "JAMAIQUE" at 10,880-11,526 sq km across six editions 1909-1938, consistent with the polygon's 10,991-11,001 sq km, and the page explicitly separates the "JAMAIQUE: CAIMANS" sub-label (Cayman Islands, routed separately to CYM-1800-2025) from the main Jamaica line — ruling out the sub-territory fold-up failure mode. Staple magnitudes (cacao ~2,687t, coffee ~3,971t, cotton lint ~96ha, oranges ~1,435t, grapefruit ~5,018t) are all plausible smallholder-plantation output for an island of ~11,000 km2, with no entrepot/re-export red flags. No annexation, cession, or occupation affected Jamaica in this period, so territory is constant across the whole observed span.

Saint Vincent and the Grenadines is a small Caribbean island group (~150 sq mi / 388 km²) that has been a single British colonial administrative unit since 1833 without any territorial change (annexation, cession, or partition) through independence in 1979 and to the present. The IIA data span (1909-1945) falls entirely within this constant-territory colonial period, well before independence, so there is no union/empire-scope ambiguity (unlike e.g. federations) and no boundary-vintage issue. The reported crop magnitudes (cotton lint ~300 ha, cotton seed ~900 ha, cacao ~120 ha, sugar ~1,500 tonnes) are plausible for a tiny island colony's agricultural output and show no discontinuities suggesting a scope change. The wiki page (draft status) is thin on the 1909-1945 territorial question specifically but its core geographic facts (island group, colonial status, no land boundaries, constant identity) are corroborated by general historical knowledge of Caribbean colonial administration, not just the page's own assertions. The page's genuine finding is a COW/polygon code-swap issue with LCA, which is unrelated to this data-routing verdict.

The assertion routes Mitchell's "japan" agricultural series (1851-1894, 231 rows, staples like rice paddy ~4.5M t, cattle ~910k head, barley/wheat/rye hectares) to JPN-1800-1895. The candidate's wiki page (draft status, 5 source citations from Biger 1995) documents Japan across this exact span as the home islands only (~370,776-377,657 km2), with no territorial change until the Treaty of Shimonoseki (17 April 1895) brought Taiwan/Pescadores/Liaodong into the successor polity JPN-1895-1945. The observed span (1851-1894) ends exactly at the pre-Shimonoseki boundary, and the neighbor_segments show 1895-1944 correctly routes to the successor — confirming our period split aligns with the actual territorial change and the source's reporting basis. The magnitudes (rice paddy, cattle, cereal hectares) are plausible in scale for Meiji-era home-islands Japan, not for a larger colonial aggregate. No sub-territory fold-up, entrepot, or union-scope issue applies here — Japan was not part of a union and the label is a national one matching a national candidate. Territory was constant across the entire observed span, so verified_equal applies.

review.basis: I re-pulled the underlying rows from the consolidated layer-B file (/home/usuario/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.csv, source=mitchell, iso3c=jpn) rather than trusting the bundle summary. The label is the whole country ("japan"), not a component, so no sub-territory fold-up; the items are domestic staples (rice, barley, wheat, sweet potatoes, tea, tobacco, livestock), so no entrepot/re-export risk. Scope test (empire vs Japan proper): rice paddy runs 3.60 Mt (1873) to 6.28 Mt (1894), then 5.99 Mt (1895) and 5.44 Mt (1896) from the successor-row years — smooth across our 1895 split, with no step of the size Taiwan (~0.5-0.7 Mt then) or later Korea would produce, so Mitchell's "japan" is Japan proper throughout and stays so after 1895 (colonies tabulated separately). Absolute magnitudes fit the home islands: ~4.5 Mt rice (~30-40 million koku, matching Meiji official crop statistics), ~2.7 Mha total cereal area, ~1 million cattle — all consistent with ~370,000 km2 and ~35-40 million people, and far too small for an empire including Taiwan/Korea. Combined reporting and boundary-vintage misdating are therefore not in play. I mark best_available rather than verified_equal for one reason only: the reporting territory did not stay constant across the observed 1851-1894 span — Japan acquired the Kurils by the 1875 Treaty of St Petersburg (relinquishing Sakhalin), annexed the Bonins (1876) and Ryukyu as Okinawa prefecture (1879), and Hokkaido was only progressively incorporated after 1869 — so no single fixed polygon (the candidate's cshapes vintage is 1886) can equal the reporting territory over the whole span, even though these additions are ~1% of area and cannot move the magnitudes. The wiki page is a draft but reasonably substantive (3.4 KB, 5 biger-1995 citations) and its core territorial claim (home islands only until Shimonoseki) is what my magnitude and continuity evidence independently supports; I did not rely on it for the verdict. Separately, three item-level data-quality problems in these rows are worth recording, none of them territorial: "rye" at a median 581,000 ha is agronomically impossible for Japan (essentially no rye grown) and matches naked barley (hadaka mugi) area instead; "oil, soybean" at ~500,000 t 1888-1894 is implausible as oil and looks like soybean grain; and the cattle series jumps 962,000 (1879) to 2,153,000 (1880), stays ~2.1 million to 1894, then reverts to 1.15 million in 1896 on a different source table (page_37 vs page_32), so the 1880-1894 cattle block is roughly double the historically attested ~1.0-1.2 million and looks like a table-extraction defect, not a territorial change.
review.wiki_note: Mitchell rows routed here (1851-1894) are Japan proper on Meiji official statistics, corroborated independently of this page: rice paddy 3.60 Mt (1873) to 6.28 Mt (1894) continues smoothly into 5.99 Mt (1895)/5.44 Mt (1896) under the successor row, so no colonial-scope break at Shimonoseki. Three data-quality defects in these rows: the series ingested as "rye" (median 581,000 ha) is almost certainly naked barley, since Japan grew essentially no rye; "oil, soybean" (~500,000 t, 1888-1894) is implausible as oil and looks like soybean grain; and cattle steps from 962,000 (1879) to 2,153,000 (1880) and holds ~2.1 million to 1894 before reverting to 1.15 million in 1896 on a different source table (page_37 vs page_32), i.e. the 1880-1894 cattle block is about double the attested ~1.0-1.2 million and is an extraction artefact, not a territorial change. Also note the page's "home islands remained the sole territory throughout" glosses over real in-span additions (Kurils 1875, Bonins 1876, Ryukyu/Okinawa 1879, progressive Hokkaido incorporation) — immaterial for magnitudes (~1% of area) but the reason this routing is best_available rather than a constant-territory match.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes IIA (International Institute of Agriculture yearbook) "belgium" agricultural data, 1909-1945 (230 rows, 34 distinct years), to BEL-1831-2025. Belgium is a genuine national agricultural producer of the listed items (butter, eggs, fertilizer, flax, grapes, sugar beet, hemp) — no entrepot/re-export or sub-territory fold-up concern; this is a straightforward national-label match, not a component or empire-scope case. The candidate wiki page (draft status but citing an external source, biger-1995, not merely its own prior assertions) documents that Belgium's territory was NOT constant across this span: it gained Eupen-Malmedy from Germany in 1919 (~1,036 km² of ~30,500 km², ~3.4%), a genuine mid-span annexation via the Treaty of Versailles, independently corroborated (biger-1995 is a boundary-history reference, not a draft-page assertion). The 1940-1944 WWII occupation (during which Germany re-annexed Eupen-Malmedy) is also within this span, per COW dates cited on the page (occupation gap 1940-05-28 to 1945-06-26), though the IIA reporting likely continued on pre-occupation borders during those war years given data continuity (37 possible years, 34 observed). Because the reporting territory did not stay constant across the full 1909-1945 span (1919 annexation, WWII occupation/re-annexation), this cannot be verified_equal even though BEL-1831-2025 is clearly the correct and only applicable candidate — it is best_available. No existing granular polity exists for pre-1919 vs post-1919 Belgium, so a split_reroute is not warranted (WHEP's own polity-definition rule treats this as within-row per the wiki's own open question, and no finer-grained existing polity exists to split against).

The assertion covers "Sweden" in FAO 1952 for 1937-1951, routed to SWE-1905-2025 (Sweden proper, post-union-with-Norway, stable metropolitan borders since 7 June 1905). Sweden was neutral in WWII and underwent no territorial change, annexation, cession, or occupation during 1937-1951 -- this is well-established historical fact independent of the wiki page (no wartime border changes for Sweden are documented anywhere; it remained the same 1905-bordered state through and beyond this span). The wiki page (draft status) corroborates this externally-verifiable stability (CShapes single polygon 1905-06-07 to 2019-12-31, no split events in the window) but the verdict does not rest on the page alone -- it rests on general historical knowledge that Sweden's borders were unchanged 1937-1951. Staple magnitudes (oats, mixed grain hectares; meat tonnes) are plausible for Sweden's agricultural scale and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change. The population figure (median 703k) is anomalously low for Sweden's true ~6.3M population in this era, but the bundle's source_conventions entry already resolves this: FAO 1952's "population" item code conflates five distinct indicators (total, agricultural, agricultural-occupied, male/female splits) under one item code, and 703k is consistent with an agricultural-occupied-type indicator, not evidence of a territorial mismatch. This is a data-interpretation issue already flagged, not a territory issue.</basis>

The candidate CHL-1902-2025 is Chile with stable borders from 1902 onward (COW ccode=155, CShapes polygon); the wiki page (reviewed status, 5 source citations from biger-1995) documents that Chile's boundaries were fully settled well before the observed span — the Peru border was delimited by treaty in 1929, and no territorial change is recorded between then and 2025. The FAO 1952 assertion's observed span (1935-1951) falls entirely within this stable-border period, so there is no annexation/cession/occupation event to worry about for a national-scale South American state. The staple magnitudes (meat ~74k tonnes, lentils ~18k ha, phosphate rock ~18k tonnes, population ~596k median — the population figure is explained by source_conventions as likely an agricultural-occupied or partial indicator subset of the fao1952 5-way population series, not a territorial anomaly) are all plausible in scale for mainland Chile and show no sign of sub-territory fold-up, entrepot re-export, or combined-reporting (no other Chilean successor/predecessor state overlaps this span). \"Chile\" as an FAO reporting label in this era is unambiguous — no union, no colonial administrative inclusion, no split polity. Confirming as verified_equal since the reporting territory equals the candidate's and stayed constant across the whole 1935-1951 span.

FAO 1952's "United Kingdom" label denotes the metropolitan UK (England+Scotland+Wales+Northern Ireland), consistent with standard FAO/statistical-yearbook practice of reporting UK agricultural production separately from its colonies/dependencies (which FAO 1952 reports under their own labels, e.g. individual colonies). The candidate GBR-1921-2025 covers exactly this metropolitan territory, stable since the December 1922 Irish Free State separation (per CShapes polygon transition documented on the wiki page) through the observed span 1937-1951 — well within the row's 1921-2025 bracket and with no territorial change in that window (no WWII-era annexation/cession affecting the UK itself; Ireland already separated a decade prior). The reported staple magnitudes (meat ~349k tonnes, oats ~1,668k hectares, poultry ~1,814k heads) are plausible in scale for UK domestic agriculture, not indicative of a broader (empire-wide) or narrower (single-region) reporting scope. The wiki page, while status=draft, carries independently checkable citations (CShapes polygon scope, COW state-system continuity) rather than being a bare CSV-derived stub, and its territorial narrative is corroborated by well-known external history (Anglo-Irish Treaty 1921, Irish Free State formalized Dec 1922) — not treated as self-evidencing.</basis>
