review.basis: Reconstructing the territory first: the UK's metropolitan borders were fixed from 6 Dec 1922 (Irish Free State secession) and did not change at any point in 1937-1951 — no annexation, cession, separation or occupation; the colonial empire was never part of the metropolitan reporting unit. So a single polity can equal the reporting territory for the whole span, provided the label means the UK proper. I tested that directly against the source rows in consolidated_layer_b.parquet (source=fao1952, country="United Kingdom", 227 rows, 1937-1951 plus prewar-average rows with null year). Two decisive scope tests: (1) "use total" land area 1951 = 24,401 thousand ha = 244,010 km2, which is the UK including Northern Ireland (244,820 km2 less the separately listed Channel Islands 194 km2 and Isle of Man 572 km2 = 244,054); Great Britain alone would be ~229,850 km2 and any Ireland-inclusive figure ~314,000 km2. (2) population total 1937 = 47,289k and 1951 = 50,558k, matching UK mid-1937 (~47.3M) and the 1951 UK census (~50.2-50.3M); GB alone in 1951 was ~48.9M, and empire scope would be hundreds of millions. Crop magnitudes agree: oats area 1949 = 1,316 kha (UK ~3.3M acres: GB ~1.17 Mha + NI ~0.14 Mha), hops area 9 kha (~22,000 acres, the English hop belt) — dimensionally and agronomically right for the UK, with no colonial-scale tropical commodity under the label, so no empire fold-in and no entrepot effect. Fold-DOWN was checked explicitly and is clean: the same source carries separate labels "United Kingdom Great Britain" (1949 tractor stock 293,230; GB-only agricultural-occupied population 1,258k in 1937), "Great Britain", "United Kingdom Channel Islands", "United Kingdom Isle of Man" and "United Kingdom dependent territories", and the Irish state sits under its own label "Ireland" (oats area 278 kha in 1949) — so "United Kingdom" is neither a component of a larger unit nor an aggregate absorbing Ireland or the crown dependencies. Boundary vintage is a non-issue because the territory is unchanged across the span; the 1937-1939 rows and prewar averages are on the same borders as 1947-1951. The candidate page's territorial claim (UK = England + Scotland + Wales + Northern Ireland, borders stable since partition) is corroborated by these independent magnitudes rather than taken on faith, so verified_equal holds for the full observed span.
review.wiki_note: Quantified territory the page lacks (polygon_area_km2 is null): FAO 1952 states the UK's total area as 24,401 thousand ha = 244,010 km2 for 1951 and its population as 47,289k (1937) / 50,558k (1951), i.e. Great Britain + Northern Ireland excluding the Channel Islands (194 km2) and Isle of Man (572 km2), which that source lists separately. Also a polygon risk worth checking: polygon_feature_year is 1921, and per the page's own account the CShapes 1921-12-06 to 1922-12-05 row is the transitional all-Ireland geometry (42.95 sq deg) rather than the post-Free-State UK (33.59 sq deg); if the transitional feature was assigned, the GBR-1921-2025 polygon overstates the territory by roughly the ~70,000 km2 of the Irish Free State and overlaps IRL-1921-2025.

Treat "United Kingdom Great Britain"/"Great Britain" rows as a NARROWER unit that must not be summed with the "United Kingdom" rows.

verdict.basis: The 'kenya' label in Mitchell routes by ISO to KEN-1926-1963 (Kenya Colony, formed by the 1926 protectorate order transferring Rudolf Province from Uganda, ending at independence 12 Dec 1963). The observed span 1926-1960 sits entirely inside this candidate's 1926-1963 territorial phase, and the draft wiki page (sourced to Biger 1995, 7 citations) documents only minor boundary amendments in 1927/1933/1936, not a scope change, so the reporting territory was constant across the observed span. Staple magnitudes are plausible for national-scale colonial Kenya (wheat ~103,000 ha highlands cultivation, coffee ~13,300 t, tea ~6,000 t, sugar cane ~9,000 ha) — consistent with a whole-colony reporting unit, not a sub-territory or an entrepot re-export figure. The neighbor_segments chain (1902-1905→KEN-1902-1907, 1908-1923→KEN-1907-1924, 1924-1925→KEN-1924-1926, 1926-1960→this candidate) is an unbroken predecessor sequence with no gaps or overlaps, supporting continuity rather than a routing seam. No combined-reporting risk (Kenya was administered separately from Uganda/Tanganyika for statistical purposes under British East Africa) and no sub-territory fold-up (Kenya here is the full national-scale colony, matching candidate_meta polity_type=national).

The FAO 1952 "Philippines" label for 1937-1951 reports on the Philippine archipelago as a single national unit — the same territory as candidate PHL-1800-2025. The item sample (abaca, agaves, bananas, buffaloes, cacao) and staple magnitudes (abaca ~174k ha, meat ~42k tonnes, poultry ~72k heads) are exactly the crops/livestock the Philippines is known for at plausible national scale — abaca in particular is a Philippine specialty crop (the country was historically the dominant world producer), not a sign of sub-territory fold-up or entrepot re-export. The 1937-1951 span straddles the Commonwealth period, the Japanese occupation (1942-1945), and independence (1946), all of which changed sovereignty/governance but not the archipelago's physical land extent — no annexation, cession, or partition occurred to this territory in that window. The candidate's wiki page (draft, thin at 2589 bytes but internally coherent) explicitly states the polygon extent is unchanged 1800-2025 and that 1898/1946 splits were considered and rejected because they record sovereignty changes only, not territorial ones — consistent with independent knowledge that the Philippines' national boundaries have been stable since the Treaty of Paris fixed the archipelago's extent. No combined-reporting, vintage-mismatch, or scope-fold-up signal is present.

The assertion routes FAO-1952 "Uruguay" agricultural/livestock series (1937-1951) to URY-1828-2025. Uruguay has had internationally stable, unchanged borders since the 1828 Treaty of Montevideo through the present (well-documented historical fact, corroborated externally, not just by the draft wiki page); there is no union/empire scope issue (unlike Sweden-Norway or Cisleithania), no combined-reporting risk (Uruguay was never merged with another FAO reporting unit), and no sub-territory fold-up (Uruguay is itself the reporting unit, not a province of something larger). The staple magnitudes (meat ~168k tonnes, rice paddy ~16k ha, sunflower seed ~82k ha, linseed ~141k ha) are all plausible in scale for Uruguay's small temperate agricultural economy and show no discontinuity that would flag a territorial-scope change across 1937-1951. The source_conventions note in the bundle (about FAO 1952's five population indicators sharing one item code) is not directly relevant to this crop/livestock assertion but confirms the source is generally reliable when read carefully by indicator. The wiki page is 'draft' status and its territorial claim (stable borders) is corroborated independently by well-known Uruguayan political history and by Biger 1995's area figure, so I am not relying on the draft page alone.

Cyprus 1937-1951 FAO1952 rows fall entirely within the pre-1974 period, during which Cyprus was under unified British colonial administration over the whole island (Crown Colony from 1925, following military occupation from 1878) with no border changes. The candidate CYP-1879-2025 wiki page documents this explicitly and notes the only territorial complication (1974 Turkish occupation/TRNC partition) postdates the observed span entirely, so it is irrelevant here. I independently verified magnitudes against the raw layer_b parquet: the bundle's misleading "population median 68k" is the agricultural-occupied indicator, not total population; the actual 'population total' indicator gives 371k (1937) and 491k (1951), both plausible for whole-island Cyprus (1931 census ~347k, 1946 census ~450k) and consistent across the two years with no discontinuity. This corroborates (rather than merely repeats) the wiki's claim of a stable, whole-island reporting territory for this span, and matches the already-recorded source_convention about the FAO1952 population series' five mixed indicators.

review.basis: I went to the underlying rows in consolidated_layer_b.parquet rather than the indicator-mixed medians in the bundle (the "median 68" population figure is the agricultural-occupied indicator, per the recorded source convention). FAO 1952 gives Cyprus "population total" 371k (1937) and 491k (1951) — essentially the island's own census trajectory (1931 census 348k, 1946 census 450k, ~494k around 1951), i.e. the reporting unit is the whole island, not a district and not any wider British-Mediterranean aggregate. Density implied, 371k/9,251 km2 = 40/km2, is right for interwar Cyprus. The production levels are equally island-scaled and agronomically characteristic of Cyprus rather than of any parent or component: grapes 52 kt (1934-38) rising to 65/63/55 kt 1949-51, wine 13-15 kt, raisins 4-20 kt, citrus (oranges 12->32 kt, grapefruit 6-7 kt), olive oil 1-4 kt, carob-belt smallholder livestock — sheep 283-304k head and goats 154-167k head against only 33-37k cattle, the classic dry-Mediterranean small-ruminant mix on a ~9,000 km2 island. Nothing is out of scale for the candidate's area, and nothing is impossibly large for the terrain (no entrepot signature: no tropical or mineral commodity is being carried under the label). No sub-territory fold-up risk (the label is the whole colony, not "Famagusta" or "Cyprus mines"), no union/empire scope issue (Cyprus was a self-contained Crown Colony, never aggregated into a wider reporting unit here), no combined reporting (one country label, one island). Boundary vintage is a non-issue: the reporting territory is an island whose extent did not change at any point in 1937-1951 — the Sovereign Base Areas were only excised at independence in 1960 and the 1974 partition is far outside the span — so the CShapes 1960 full-island polygon is exactly the reported territory and it was constant for the entire observed span, which is what verified_equal requires. The draft wiki page's territorial description (full island ~9,251 km2, stable coastline, post-1974 drift documented) is consistent with what the numbers independently show; I did not need it to reach the verdict and it is not doing load-bearing work here.

verdict.basis: The observed span (1952-1960) falls entirely before the 1972 Okinawa reversion, so the candidate's own territory (mainland Japan, excluding the US-administered Ryukyus) was constant throughout the whole span being verified, and matches Mitchell's Japan reporting territory for those years (Japanese government statistics of the period, which Mitchell compiles, excluded Okinawa/the Ryukyus until the 1972 reversion — a well-documented historical fact independent of the draft wiki page). Staple magnitudes (potatoes ~1.31M ha, sweet potatoes ~2.81M ha, barley ~0.76M ha) are plausible for mid-1950s mainland Japan agriculture and show no discontinuity vs. the preceding JPN-1945-1952 segment, consistent with unchanged reporting territory across that boundary. The candidate's later territorial change (1972 Okinawa reversion) does not affect this verdict since it lies outside the 1952-1960 window actually being asserted; the wiki page itself flags this as an open question (oq-okinawa-split-candidate) for the full 1952-2025 row, not for this sub-span.

The assertion covers "angola" as an IIA-yearbook label for 1930-1945, routed to ANG-1905-1975 (Portuguese Angola, 1905-1975, borders fixed by the 1905 Victor Emmanuel arbitration and unchanged through 1975 per CShapes 2.0). The observed span (1930-1945) sits entirely within this constant-territory colonial period with no annexation, cession, or occupation event documented for Angola in that window (Portugal held the colony continuously; no partition or border change occurred until independence in 1975, well after the span). This is a whole-country colonial label, not a sub-territory (no fold-up risk — Angola is the entire reporting unit, not a province within it), and not an entrepot/re-export case: the commodities reported (cotton lint, cotton seed, groundnuts, tobacco, sesame, coffee) are all standard interior agricultural staples for Angola's actual climate/geography, at magnitudes (thousands of tonnes) plausible for a mid-sized colonial economy — no agronomic red flags suggesting transit goods from elsewhere. The wiki page (draft status, 3 source citations from Wikipedia and CShapes) documents the constant 1905-1975 border and the colonial administrative continuity, which is independently corroborated by the CShapes polygon record (status=colony, ruler=PRT, unchanged 1905→1975) rather than relying solely on the draft's narrative — CShapes is a structured external dataset, not just prose assertion. Since the reporting territory equals the candidate's territory and did not change across the observed 1930-1945 span, this is verified_equal rather than best_available.

The IIA "congo" label routes to COG-1919-1960 (Middle Congo / Moyen-Congo, a French Equatorial Africa colonial subdivision, ~342,000 km², stable administrative unit from 1919 to 1960 per its predecessor/successor chain). The observed span (1919-1945) falls entirely within this single polity's 1919-1960 period, so no boundary change occurs within the span. The staple magnitudes (coffee 2,200t, cotton lint 7,800t, cotton seed 19,400t, cacao 1,480t, groundnuts 14,650ha) are modest, consistent with a mid-sized colonial cash-crop economy and clearly too small to represent the combined output of all French Equatorial Africa (which would also include Gabon, Chad, and Oubangui-Chari), supporting that IIA reported Moyen-Congo as its own distinct territorial unit rather than folding it into a larger AEF aggregate. The wiki page (draft status, but with 6 source citations from Biger 1995) independently documents Middle Congo as a distinct division of French Congo since 1903/1906, separate from Gabon/Chad/CAR, which corroborates rather than merely asserts the territorial scope. No annexation, cession, or administrative reorganization affecting this territory is documented within 1919-1945.

source_convention.convention: IIA yearbooks report French Equatorial Africa's constituent colonies separately; the label 'Congo' denotes Moyen-Congo (French Congo) alone, not combined AEF totals (which would also include Gabon, Chad, and Oubangui-Chari/CAR).
source_convention.evidence: Staple magnitudes (thousands of tonnes for coffee, cotton, cacao) are consistent with a single mid-sized colonial territory, not the sum of four AEF colonies; wiki page documents Moyen-Congo as administratively distinct from Gabon/Chad/CAR since 1903/1906.

verdict.basis: Assertion routes IIA "dr congo" (ISO cod, iso+prior route) 1915-1945, 220 rows/25 years, to COD-1910-1960 (Belgian Congo, 1910-1960). The wiki page (draft status but with 6 source citations to Biger 1995) documents that Belgian Congo's external borders were fixed by bilateral treaties (France, Portugal, UK) before 1910 and that no annexations or cessions occurred 1910-1960 — the observed span 1915-1945 sits entirely inside this stable sub-period, well clear of both endpoints. Staple magnitudes (cotton lint median 139,276 ha, cotton seed 91,300 ha, coffee 17,242 ha) are plausible scale for a colony the size of Belgian Congo (~2.3M km2) and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change. The label "dr congo" names the whole colonial territory, not a sub-component, so no fold-up risk; no entrepot/re-export concern for these staple crops given Congo's own agro-ecology. The one open item on the page (1908 vs 1910 start-date discrepancy) concerns the polity's founding boundary before the observed span and does not affect territorial constancy across 1915-1945.

review.basis: The label is "Congo belge" in the IIA international yearbooks, 1915-1945, entirely inside COD-1910-1960 (1910-1960), so no split-basis issue; Belgian Congo's external borders were fixed by pre-1910 treaties (the Lado enclave went to Sudan in 1910, before the span), so the reporting territory did not change within 1915-1945. I checked the two live scope risks directly in the source rows (/home/usuario/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.parquet). (a) Fold-up of Ruanda-Urundi: IIA carries Ruanda-Urundi as its OWN country line (layer B label "burundi", iso3c BDI, raw label "ruanda-urundi" per state/iia_label_provenance.csv) for 1930-1937, with exactly the same commodity set as the Congo line (cotton lint/seed, groundnuts, tobacco) — a source that reports the part separately is not folding it into the whole, so "Congo belge" is Congo proper at least over 1930-1937. The only "Includes Ruanda-Urundi" footnotes in the footnote-extraction corpus (~/Nextcloud/whep/footnote_territory/footnote_territory_claims.parquet) are FAO 1953, cotton lint / cottonseed / tractors — a different source and later years, not IIA. (b) Sub-territory narrowing: no province/district label; the magnitudes are colony-scale and internally coherent — cotton area 900 ha (1917) -> 136,553 (1930) -> 400,000 (1938) -> ~350,000 (1945), matching the documented forced-cotton expansion of the Belgian Congo, and coffee 264 ha (1915) -> 58,000 ha (1937). No step anywhere in the series that would betray a scope change, in particular none at 1938 when the separate Ruanda-Urundi line stops. Ruanda-Urundi's own IIA figures (cotton 1,327-4,000 ha) are ~1% of the Congo's, so even a silent fold-in for the 1938-1945 tail would be within noise, but I could not verify IIA's post-1937 practice from the publication itself (web searches on IIA yearbook country conventions returned nothing usable), so I record this as best_available rather than verified_equal. No entrepot concern: cotton, coffee, cacao, palm and rubber are all genuinely Congolese output.
review.wiki_note: IIA reports Ruanda-Urundi as a separate country line for 1930-1937 (same crop set as the Congo line), so IIA "Congo belge" 1915-1945 is Congo proper, not the Congo+Ruanda-Urundi union; residual unverified risk only for the 1938-1945 tail, where no separate Ruanda-Urundi line exists (worth <=1-2% of Congo cotton area). Relatedly, the CODRU-1922-1960 page's claim that "FAO/IIA footnotes flag combined reporting" overstates the evidence: the only "Includes Ruanda-Urundi" footnotes in the extraction corpus are FAO 1953 (cotton lint, cottonseed, tractors) — none are IIA — which also bears on this page's dec-cod-alias-fao1952 decision routing FAO "Belgian Congo" to COD alone.

The three "Includes Ruanda-Urundi" footnotes in ~/Nextcloud/whep/footnote_territory/footnote_territory_claims.parquet are all source=fao, year=1953.

verdict.basis: Assertion routes IIA label "austria" (1919-1945, 219 rows) to AUT-1919-2025. The wiki page (draft, but well-sourced with COW citations) explicitly flags the Anschluss gap (1938-03-13 to 1955-07-27, Austria absorbed into Nazi Germany, then occupied) as an open question about whether this row should be split — so I checked territorial continuity directly rather than trusting the draft's routing. Independent evidence in data/final/source_stated_area_basis.csv shows the IIA source itself reports Austria's stated area as ~83,845 km2 consistently across editions 1909, 1925, 1929, 1932, 1933, AND 1938 (ratio 1.002 vs polygon area, flagged "agrees") — i.e. even in the Anschluss year the yearbook kept reporting Austria on its own First-Republic territorial basis, not folded into Greater Germany. The wiki's own verification note (for a different source, `juan` crop-area data) independently corroborates stability 1919-1960 with no step at 1938 or 1945. No IIA stated-area edition is available for 1939-1945 to directly confirm continuity through the rest of the war, but no counter-evidence of a territorial break exists either. Given the source's reporting territory did not visibly change size, I confirm the routing, but because a real annexation/occupation event (1938-1955) sits inside the observed span and the last confirmed edition is 1938 (not 1945), I use best_available rather than verified_equal per the mid-span-history rule.
verdict.wiki_note: data/final/source_stated_area_basis.csv shows the IIA source itself (not just the `juan` source cited in the current verification note) reports Austria's stated area as ~83,845 km2 across editions 1909-1938, including the 1938 Anschluss-year edition (ratio 1.002 vs polygon, "agrees") — direct source-level evidence that IIA kept reporting Austria on its pre-Anschluss territorial basis rather than folding it into Greater Germany. No IIA edition after 1938 is available to confirm continuity through 1939-1945, so this should be treated as best_available, not verified_equal, for the 1938-1945 portion of the span.

verdict.basis: Switzerland's metropolitan borders have been stable since 1815 (Congress of Vienna), confirmed by Biger 1995's citation that "the northern boundary of Switzerland has never been changed" since then, with only a trivial 1862 Dappes valley exchange with France. The assertion's span (1909-1945) falls entirely within this stable-border era: no WWI or WWII occupation or territorial change occurred (Switzerland maintained neutrality throughout both wars, unlike Belgium/France). COW state-system data shows continuous tenure 1816-2024 with no breaks. CShapes' single static polygon corroborates. The IIA "switzerland" label denotes metropolitan Switzerland with no colonial possessions or union partners to create scope ambiguity, so there is no union/empire-scope or sub-territory fold-up issue. Staple magnitudes (wine ~40kt, sugar ~7.6kt, eggs ~22kt) are plausible in scale for Switzerland's population (~4M in this period) and agricultural profile, showing no discontinuity suggestive of a scope change. The wiki page, while status=draft, is well-sourced (10 citations) on exactly the territorial-stability question needed here, so I treat its Biger-1995 citations as corroborating evidence rather than the sole basis.

Assertion covers FAO 1952 "Yugoslavia" label for 1947-1951, routed to F248-1947-1991 (SFRY, 1947-1991, ~255,000 km², COW 345). The candidate's own draft wiki page documents that this row's territory was fixed by the 1947-02-10 Paris Peace Treaty (Istria/Zadar/Trieste Zone B acquisitions from Italy) and remained constant until the next boundary event (1954 Trieste Zone B administration, formalized 1975) and ultimately the 1991 dissolution -- both well outside the observed 1947-1951 span. So within the whole observed span the reporting territory is the same, single, unchanging SFRY territory the candidate represents; there is no mid-span annexation/cession affecting 1947-1951. The neighbor_segments entry (1937-1939 -> F248-1920-1947, the pre-war Kingdom of Yugoslavia row) confirms our own period split lands the boundary change correctly at 1947, and the FAO figures (cattle, buffaloes, sugar, fertilizers, dry beans, hemp, soybeans) are unremarkable in scale for a ~255,000 km² Balkan agrarian state -- no entrepot or scale-implausibility red flags. The source_conventions note in the bundle (verified 2026-08-14) already establishes that this source's population-series artifacts are indicator-mixing defects unrelated to territorial scope, which further supports that the label is reporting one consistent SFRY territory rather than a shifting one. The wiki page is draft (unreviewed, 0 source_citations per its metadata) so its claims are treated as a hypothesis, but its specific dates/events (1947 Paris Peace Treaty territorial cession, no boundary change again until 1954/1975/1991) match well-established Cold-War-era Yugoslav historical geography and are corroborated by the data's own magnitude plausibility and the correct neighbor-segment split at 1947 -- independent enough to confirm rather than merely echo the draft.

Guatemala's national territory was settled by the collapse of the Federal Republic of Central America (late 1830s) and remained constant through the entire 1884-1960 observed span -- no annexations, cessions, or occupations affected its core territory in this period (the only territorial dispute, over Belize, was a claim never under Guatemalan administrative control, so it does not affect the reporting basis of a national statistical source like Mitchell). The commodity mix and magnitudes (coffee, cotton, sugar, cattle, milk, beer) are exactly what is expected of a small Central American agricultural economy of Guatemala's size and population in this era, with no sign of entrepot/re-export inflation or sub-national fold-up. The wiki page (draft status) documents the constant-territory rationale explicitly, which is corroborated by general historical knowledge of Central American independence borders, so I treat the territorial claim as independently supportable rather than merely citing the draft page circularly.

review.basis: Reconstructing the territory first: the Republic of Guatemala's administered extent was fixed before the observed span opens. The Chiapas/Soconusco question with Mexico was settled by the treaty of 27 Sept 1882 (demarcation completed in the 1890s), i.e. prior to 1884; the British Honduras (Belize) claim was never administered territory of Guatemala at any point in the span, so it does not enter the reporting base; and the only live territorial dispute inside the span, with Honduras over the Motagua/Amatique/Golfo Dulce region, was resolved by the Hughes arbitral award of 23 Jan 1933 substantially on the basis of Guatemala's existing effective occupation, so it confirmed rather than changed the territory actually administered and reported on. Guatemala held no overseas dependencies and was in no union or federation after the 1830s, so there is no union/empire-scope, colonial-inclusion or combined-reporting failure mode here. On the label side, "Guatemala" in Mitchell (International Historical Statistics: The Americas) is a sovereign-state series, not a province, district or plantation aggregate, so the sub-territory fold-up direction is clean; and the commodities are agronomically native to the territory (green coffee, cane sugar, cotton, cattle/milk/meat), so this is production, not entrepot re-export. Magnitudes corroborate a country of ~109,000 km2 with a mid-century population of 2-3 million: raw centrifugal sugar median 33,000 t, meat 35,000 t, whole fresh cow milk 175,000 t, beer 7,600 t, cottonseed 6,000 t — all in the right order of magnitude for Guatemala proper and far too small for any Central American federation reading. No neighbour segments and no competing period splits exist (the candidate is a single 1821-2025 row), so there is no split-basis or continuity-step problem to test. The candidate's wiki page is draft and rests only on Biger 1995, so I did not rely on it for the territorial claim; it was corroborated independently from the 1882 treaty and 1933 award record.
review.wiki_note: The Summary states the 1823 United Provinces of Central America comprised "Honduras, Guatemala, Nicaragua, and Belize" — Belize was never a member (it was British-administered); the federation was Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica. Also missing from Territorial extent: the two events that actually fix Guatemala's boundaries within the data span — the 1882 boundary treaty with Mexico (Soconusco/Chiapas, demarcated to the 1890s) and the Hughes arbitral award of 23 Jan 1933 settling the Honduras boundary along the Motagua largely per Guatemala's effective occupation, which is why the territory can be treated as constant 1884-1960 despite the 1886 polygon vintage.

verdict.basis: Assertion routes FAO-1952 "Switzerland" (1936-1951, 210 rows: butter, meat, cattle, horses/mules/asses, commercial phosphoric acid, population) to CHE-1800-2025. The wiki page (draft status, but substantive: 5580 bytes, 10 source citations, no TODO markers) documents via Biger 1995 that Switzerland's borders have been essentially unchanged since 1815 ("the northern boundary of Switzerland has never been changed"; only a minor 1862 Dappes valley exchange with France), corroborated independently by CShapes recording a single static polygon and COW listing continuous state-system tenure 1816-2024 with no WWII occupation gap (Switzerland stayed neutral). This is a metropolitan, non-federal, non-colonial national label with no union/empire-scope ambiguity (unlike Sweden-Norway or Cisleithania), no sub-territory fold-up (Switzerland is not a component of anything), and no plausible entrepot/re-export distortion for cattle, meat, butter, or horses/mules/asses at this small alpine country's normal domestic-production scale. The population median of 402k (n=10) is not a territorial red flag: per the bundle's already-verified source_convention, FAO-1952 population under one item code mixes total/agricultural/agricultural-occupied indicators, and ~400k is squarely in range for Switzerland's agricultural-occupied population (~8-9% of its ~4.7M total in 1950), not evidence of a smaller reporting territory. Since Swiss borders were constant across the entire 1936-1951 span and match the candidate's documented full-period territory, this is a straightforward confirm with verified_equal.

The candidate DOM-1800-2025 is the single continuous Dominican Republic polity (1800-2025, no splits in the DB). Its wiki page (draft status, but with 6 source citations from Biger 1995, an independent geographic reference) documents the territory as the eastern portion of Hispaniola, ~48,443 km2, bounded by Haiti to the west (358km border) - a stable definition since the 1865 War of Restoration. The observed span (1901-1960) postdates that stabilization; the 1916-1924 US occupation was an administrative intervention, not a territorial change, and the Dominican-Haitian border treaties of 1929/1935 were demarcations of the existing line, not cessions/annexations. Mitchell's 'Dominican Republic' label in this era denotes the sovereign state itself, not a union or sub-territory. Staple magnitudes (sugar ~366,000 t/yr median, cacao ~22,000 t/yr) are consistent with a country of this size and its known role as a Caribbean sugar/cacao exporter - no entrepot or agronomic-impossibility red flags, and no evidence of combined reporting with another territory. No neighbor_segments data was available to cross-check continuity, but the historical record for the DR in this period shows no boundary change, so I treat the reporting territory as constant and equal to the candidate's for the whole span.

The candidate IND-1937-1947 is British India after the Burma separation (1 Apr 1937, Government of Burma Act 1935) and before Partition (15 Aug 1947), with Portuguese/French Indian enclaves subtracted (both were foreign sovereign territory throughout this span, per the 2026-08-13 polygon fix documented on the page). CShapes records no intermediate boundary change for gwcode=750 across the whole 1937-1947 span, and the source's observed years (1937-1946) fall entirely inside that constant-border window, well clear of both the Burma and Partition boundary dates. Mitchell's 'India' label for these years is the standard historiographical unit (undivided British India post-Burma, pre-Partition) and its staple magnitudes (rice paddy median ~34Mt, wheat ~11.2Mt) are of the right order for undivided British India's agricultural output in this period, showing no discontinuity that would suggest a scope mismatch. The wiki page (wiki_status: draft, but substantively sourced with 9 citations to CShapes-2.0, COW state-system, and Biger 1995) independently establishes the constant-territory conclusion for this exact span rather than merely asserting it, so it corroborates rather than launders the verdict.
verdict.wiki_note: Neither the page nor the assertion bundle addresses whether Mitchell's 'India' production series for 1937-1946 include output from the princely states (nominally under British paramountcy but not administratively absorbed, and included in the row's polygon) or cover British-administered provinces only. Pre-1947 Indian colonial agricultural statistics are frequently province-based and may under-cover princely-state production; this is a potential sub-territory fold-up worth flagging for future review if finer provenance on Mitchell's underlying colonial-yearbook sources becomes available, though the observed magnitudes are not obviously inconsistent with either scope.

verdict.basis: The wiki page (draft) only documents FAO-1952 "Gold Coast and British Togoland" routing for 1949-1951; it says nothing about IIA data or the 1909-1945 span, so it cannot support this assertion on its own (page_inadequate). Independent evidence in pipelines/polity-autoimprove/state/iia_label_provenance.csv is decisive against a clean confirm: the layer-B label "ghana" is fed by THREE distinct raw IIA labels -- "gold coast", "british togo", AND "french togo" (kind=shares_target,3) -- and value-fingerprint measurement (territory_signal=redirected, not clean) finds the DOMINANT contributor (63% share) is "german togoland", i.e. undivided/Togoland-era data, not Gold Coast Colony data. The companion row for raw label "togo" shows german togoland at 100% dominant share, confirming "german togoland" is a real, heavily-duplicated raw series in this extract, not a spec artifact. French Togoland was never part of Gold Coast/Ghana under any administration (it is FTO-1920-1960, a separate existing polity that became independent Togo in 1960); German Togoland (1884-1920, GTO-1884-1920) predates the Gold Coast/Togo split entirely and is unrelated to Gold Coast territory. Only British Togoland's post-1920 fusion with Gold Coast is a documented, accepted approximation (and even that has its own dedicated aggregate polity, GCT-1919-1956 "Gold Coast and British Togoland", which this routing bypasses). With ~63% of the pooled "ghana" values fingerprint-matching a non-Ghana territory, and the 1909-1919 portion of the span predating any Togo administrative link to Gold Coast at all, I cannot confirm the reporting territory equals GHA-1898-1957's for the whole 1909-1945 span, nor can I cleanly tile a split without row-level year/label detail I don't have access to (layer B lives outside this repo). This is exactly the graceful "uncertain" case: strong evidence of combined/foreign-territory contamination, insufficient granularity to assign a corrected route with confidence.
verdict.wiki_note: The page documents only FAO-1952 "Gold Coast and British Togoland" routing (1949-1951); it says nothing about this IIA assertion's 1909-1945 span. External evidence (pipelines/polity-autoimprove/state/iia_label_provenance.csv) shows layer-B's "ghana" label pools THREE raw IIA labels -- gold coast, british togo, AND french togo -- with territory_signal=redirected and a 63% dominant-share fingerprint match to "german togoland" (undivided pre-1920 Togoland data, unrelated to Gold Coast). French Togoland (now FTO-1920-1960/independent Togo) was never part of Gold Coast under any administration, so its inclusion here is a likely combined-reporting/foreign-territory contamination the page does not address. Also worth noting: a dedicated aggregate polity GCT-1919-1956 ("Gold Coast and British Togoland") already exists in the DB and is not being used by this routing decision.

review.basis: Numbers first. I pulled the 102 raw IIA rows for country=="ghana" from ~/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.csv rather than trusting the bundle's summary (which is itself misleading: it pools the `ha` and `tonnes` rows into one median, so "cotton lint: median 1,700 tonnes (n=35)" mixes 10,000-24,000 ha area rows with 18-2,500 t output rows; the true lint tonnage series is 18-36 t for 1909-1921 and 767-2,500 t for 1922-24/1939-45). The decisive series is cocoa: area 355,000 ha (1922) rising monotonically to 486,000 ha (1941-44), with production values of 238,871 / 249,300 / 265,100 t. That level is only compatible with the ENTIRE Gold Coast dependency — the interwar world's largest cocoa producer, ~40% of world output, record 311,000 t in 1936 including 20,000+ t (6.75%) from British Mandated Togoland, 257,000 t exported 1938, 228,000 t in 1944-45 (AEHN WP-8; Hansard 1946/1948). So the sub-territory fold-up failure family is ruled out in the strong direction: this is NOT Gold Coast Colony proper, Ashanti, or a district — a component would be a small fraction of these figures. Ancillary series are internally coherent at colony scale and cheap by comparison (groundnuts 95-130 t on 150-160 ha ~700 kg/ha in the 1920s, stepping to 4,000-7,200 t on 10,000-18,000 ha in 1935-37 — the Northern Territories groundnut expansion / improved enumeration, not a territorial change; cotton 767-1,651 t lint on 10,847-21,000 ha ~70-80 kg/ha, normal rain-fed African cotton). No entrepot signature: cocoa, cotton and groundnuts at these levels are agronomically native to this territory. No magnitude discontinuity anywhere in 1909-1945 that would suggest a scope change; the one visible break (cocoa 1922 -> 1941, +37%) is planting expansion, smooth and monotonic. What keeps this from being verified_equal is the Togoland question, which the arithmetic cannot settle. German Togoland was occupied in 1914 and the British sphere became a mandate administered as an integral part of the Gold Coast from 1920 (common customs, common budget), and colonial cocoa totals of the era conventionally include it — the 6.75% Togoland share is quoted as a share OF the Gold Coast total. So the reporting territory in 1909-1919 is almost certainly Gold Coast proper and in ~1920-1945 most likely Gold Coast + British Togoland: it did not stay constant across the observed span, which by the stated rule forces best_available. WHEP already has GCT-1919-1956 "Gold Coast and British Togoland" (239,046 km², aggregate) as an existing polity, so a split_reroute (1909-1919 -> GHA-1898-1957, 1920-1945 -> GCT-1919-1956) is a live alternative; I did not take it because I could not establish IIA's own convention for this label from the source documentation, the Togoland increment (~7% of cocoa) is inside the noise of these series so the data cannot arbitrate, and the existing page has already deliberately routed the analogous fao1952 "Gold Coast and British Togoland" labels to GHA-1898-1957 rather than to GCT — rerouting IIA alone would make the database internally inconsistent. GHA-1898-1957 is the correct and best available home for this label; I flag the GCT question rather than resolving it. Separately the page is wrong on areas (see wiki_note), which does not change the routing but does undercut it as evidence.
review.wiki_note: Two corrections to this page's territorial arithmetic, plus one open routing question. (1) The page states the CShapes polygon "(~238,533 km²) covers the Gold Coast Colony proper and does NOT include British Togoland (~33,773 km²)", yet its own dec-gha-1956-hole-closed section records the Gold-Coast-proper CShapes step as 212,416.75 km². Both cannot hold. 238,533 km² is the area of MODERN Ghana, i.e. Gold Coast INCLUDING former British Togoland (Ghana 238,535; British Togoland ~33,776; Gold Coast proper ~204,760). The 238,533 figure stored in polities_database.csv for the 1898 feature therefore does not describe an 1898 Gold Coast. (2) Consequently the repeated "~14% understatement" claim is self-contradictory: 238,533 + 33,773 = 272,306 km², which exceeds the 239,046 km² recorded for GCT-1919-1956, the polity that is explicitly the combined unit. The recorded area, the claimed exclusion, and the claimed understatement cannot all be true. (3) Open question this page should carry: IIA International Yearbook data 1909-1945 under label "ghana" (102 rows; cocoa 355,000-486,000 ha, ~239-265 kt) is routed here for the whole span, but from 1920 British Togoland was administered as an integral part of the Gold Coast with a common customs union, and period cocoa totals conventionally include it (British Mandated Togoland supplied >20,000 t = 6.75% of the 311,000 t 1936/7 Gold Coast total). Whether the post-1919 portion belongs to GCT-1919-1956 rather than here is unresolved; the same ambiguity affects the fao1952 combined labels this page already decided to keep here.

verdict.basis: The assertion covers "Mozambique" (ISO moz) reported by IIA for 1922-1937, routed to MOZ-1891-1975 (Portuguese Mozambique, 1891-1975). The polities_database.csv shows only one polity code spans this period for MOZ (MOZ-1800-1891 ends in 1891, MOZ-1891-1975 covers 1891-1975, MOZ-1975-2025 starts in 1975), so no alternative existing polity could better fit any part of 1922-1937 and no split is needed. The wiki page (draft, thin: 2068 bytes, 1 citation) documents Mozambique as a single Portuguese colony/overseas province from 1891 to independence in 1975, with the only territorial change event at the 1891 start (outside our span) and no further border changes noted through 1975. Portuguese Mozambique was administered and reported internationally (League of Nations/IIA statistical yearbooks) as a single colonial unit; the reported agricultural magnitudes (cotton lint/seed in the thousands of ha, sugar in tens of thousands of tonnes, modest tea and tobacco output) are plausible for the whole colony and show no sign of being a narrow sub-territory (e.g., one chartered company's concession zone) nor an entrepot reporting someone else's output. There is no evidence of any annexation, cession, or administrative split affecting Mozambique's reporting territory during 1922-1937, so the reporting territory is both equal to the candidate's and constant across the whole observed span.

Assertion routes IIA's "romania" label (1920-1939, 206 rows, national agricultural production) to ROU-1920-1940. The candidate's wiki page documents that this row spans Greater Romania at its post-Trianon maximum extent (~296,000 km²), beginning with the 4 June 1920 Treaty of Trianon border formalization and ending with the three simultaneous 1940 territorial losses (Second Vienna Award to Hungary, Soviet ultimatum ceding Bessarabia/N. Bukovina, Treaty of Craiova ceding S. Dobruja to Bulgaria) — all well-established historical events independent of the page itself. Critically, the observed data span (1920-1939) falls entirely BEFORE the 1940 losses, so the reporting territory is constant across the whole observed period and equals the candidate's declared territory. neighbor_segments corroborate this: pre-1920 segments (1918-1919) route to smaller assembling-Romania polities and 1940-1945 routes to the reduced post-loss ROU-1940-1947, consistent with the candidate being the stable "Greater Romania, uncut" interval. Staple magnitudes (wine ~606k t, sugar ~95k t, hemp yarn ~30k ha) are plausible for a large (296,000 km²) agrarian interwar state and show no discontinuity within the span. This is a whole-country label with no union/entrepot/sub-territory complications. Page is draft status but its territorial/date claims are independently verifiable historical facts, not a bare assertion.

Assertion routes Juan's ISO-coded "bolivia" agricultural series (1910-1937, ha/tonnes for barley, maize, wheat, potatoes, coffee) to BOL-1909-1938 by ISO match. The wiki page (draft, thin: 1 citation, 1856 bytes) documents this polity period as bounded by predecessor/successor splits tied to earlier territorial losses (1903-1909 Acre cession) and the Chaco War/1938 settlement — i.e. the period's own boundaries were deliberately drawn around Bolivia's stable inter-war territory, ending exactly where the Chaco War loss is formalized (1938), just past the observed span's last year (1937). Staple magnitudes (150,000 ha barley, 321,500 ha maize, 49,000 ha wheat, 293,000 ha potatoes, ~6,880 t coffee) are plausible for Bolivia's altiplano/valley agriculture at this era and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change mid-span. Neighbor segment (1938-1960 -> BOL-1938-2025) continues smoothly, consistent with the same national reporting basis before and after the formal 1938 border change. However, the Chaco War itself (1932-1935) was an active military occupation of the disputed Gran Chaco territory, falling inside the observed span (1910-1937) even though the formal cession only occurred at the 1938 treaty — this is exactly the kind of mid-span occupation event the routing guidance flags as disqualifying verified_equal, even though the reporting territory for Bolivia's own national agricultural statistics almost certainly continued to be compiled on the pre-war/de-jure basis throughout (no evidence the source switched to a de-facto occupied-territory basis). Given this, confirm but as best_available rather than verified_equal.
verdict.wiki_note: The Chaco War (1932-1935), during which Paraguay occupied most of the disputed Gran Chaco, falls inside this polity's own observed data span (1910-1937) even though formal cession only came with the 1938 treaty — the page currently frames the war only as the reason for the 1938 predecessor/successor split, not as a mid-span territorial-control event that bears on how agricultural statistics for the disputed region may have been (or not been) reported during 1932-1935.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes IIA "netherlands" 1909-1945 (203 rows, 34 distinct years — gaps consistent with WWII disruption) to NLD-1830-2025. The candidate's metropolitan European territory has been stable since the Treaty of London (1839) fixed the Dutch-Belgian border; no annexation or cession affected the Netherlands proper between 1909 and 1945. The 1940-1945 German occupation was an administrative interruption of sovereignty, not a change to the reporting territory/land area — the same country continued to be the referent, unlike cases (Alsace-Lorraine, Sudetenland) where borders themselves moved. The commodity profile in staple_magnitudes (dairy, eggs, beans, flax) is classic temperate-European agriculture, consistent with metropolitan Dutch output rather than colonial produce, which corroborates that this IIA label denotes the metropole and excludes the Netherlands East Indies (reported separately by IIA under its own colonial label) — an entrepot/fold-up concern that does not apply here. The wiki page is draft status and its claims (stable 1839+ borders) are independently corroborable general historical fact, so I am not relying on it circularly. Given territorial constancy across the whole span, this is a clean verified_equal confirm.

source_convention.convention: IIA's 'Netherlands' label denotes metropolitan (European) Netherlands only, excluding the Netherlands East Indies and other Dutch colonies, which IIA reports under separate colonial labels.
source_convention.evidence: Commodity mix (dairy/eggs/beans/flax) matches temperate Dutch agriculture, not tropical colonial produce; consistent with known IIA/FAO-predecessor practice of reporting metropoles and colonies separately.

verdict.wiki_note: IIA's 'netherlands' label for this span reports metropolitan territory only, excluding the Netherlands East Indies (reported separately by IIA under its own colonial heading) — the commodity mix (dairy, eggs, beans, flax) is temperate-European, not colonial, corroborating this. The 1940-1945 German occupation interrupted sovereignty but not the reporting territory/land area, so the span is territorially constant despite gaps in data years during active war years.

review.basis: The failure family to rule out here is union/empire scope: does the IIA's "Netherlands" mean metropolitan Netherlands or the Kingdom including the Netherlands Indies? Two independent lines settle it. (1) The IIA source itself carries a separate label for the colony — the same bundle file contains 'indonesia|iia|1909-1944' (375 rows, routed to IDN-1800-1945) and 'indonesia|iia|1945-1945'; a publication that tabulates the Indies as its own country row is not folding it into the metropole's totals. (2) Magnitudes discriminate cleanly: this label's sugar raw centrifugal median is 223,479 t, which is the well-known scale of Dutch domestic beet-sugar output in the 1910s-1930s, while the separate Indonesia label carries 1,415,377 t of cane sugar — the Java crop is not inside the Netherlands figure, so no double counting or fold-up. Eggs ~107 kt and the small grape area (1,000 ha, greenhouse/glasshouse scale) are likewise metropolitan-Dutch magnitudes, agronomically impossible to read as tropical-colony data. No sub-territory fold-up in the other direction either: the label is the whole country, not a province. Boundary vintage: metropolitan Dutch borders were fixed by the 1839 Treaty of London and unchanged through 1909-1945 (the 1940-45 German occupation was an occupation, not a cession; the small 1949 annexations fall after the span and were reverted in 1963), so the reporting territory is both equal to the candidate polygon and constant across the entire observed span — hence verified_equal rather than best_available. The draft wiki page's claim of metropolitan stability since 1839 was used only as a restatement of independently known boundary history, not as the load-bearing evidence.

verdict.basis: The fao1952 "Ireland" label rows are the 26-county state (Irish Free State/Éire/Republic), matching candidate IRL-1921-2025 exactly. The wiki page (draft status, but well-cited: 13 source citations from CShapes-2.0, COW and Biger-1995) documents a stable territory since the 1922 Irish Free State constitution with no polygon changes through 2019, explicitly excluding the 6 Ulster counties (tracked separately as GBNIR-1921-2025). Independent verification: pulling the raw fao1952 population:population total rows for Ireland gives 2,948k (1937) and 2,959k (1951) — matching the well-known 26-county Irish censuses (1936 census ~2.97M, 1951 census ~2.96M) and excluding Northern Ireland's ~1.3M, which would push the total to ~4.2-4.3M if NI were folded in. This independently confirms the label denotes the Republic/Free State only, not the whole island. The bundle's flagged "median 602" for population is an artifact of mixing five population sub-indicators under one item code (per the existing source_convention entry already in the bundle) — the true total-population series (2948/2959k) is the correct check and it matches. The observed span 1937-1951 falls entirely within Ireland's post-1922 stable borders (no annexation, cession or occupation affecting this candidate in that window), so the territory was both equal to the candidate's and constant across the whole span.
verdict.wiki_note: Independent check of the raw fao1952 total-population series for Ireland gives 2,948k (1937) and 2,959k (1951), matching the historical 26-county censuses (~2.97M in 1936, ~2.96M in 1951) and excluding Northern Ireland's population — direct quantitative confirmation that this label is the 26-county Republic/Free State, not the whole island, which the page currently asserts only via polygon/border sources and not via population data.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes FAO-1952 "Norway" labeled production/population rows (1937-1951) to NOR-1800-2025. Norway's metropolitan territory has been stable and undisputed since the 1905 dissolution of the union with Sweden (well-documented; the union ended without any territorial change, and no further territorial change occurred to Norway until well after 1951 — the World Court's 1933 ruling on East Greenland and 1944 recognition of Iceland's independence concerned overseas dependencies/former union partners, not mainland Norway). The 1940-1945 German occupation was a military occupation, not a change of Norway's own territory or its statistical reporting unit — Norway continued to be reported as Norway (government-in-exile continuity, post-war restoration of the same borders), so FAO would be using pre-war (1937) and post-war (1951) Norway on the same territorial basis. The population magnitude (median ~301k) initially looked implausible (actual Norway population ~2.9-3.2M in this era) but the bundle's source_conventions entry already resolves this: the FAO1952 "population" item code conflates five indicators (total/agricultural/agricultural-occupied/male/female splits) and a figure around 1/10 of true total for a country with a large fishing/forestry-not-agriculture workforce is consistent with the agricultural-occupied indicator, not a territorial mismatch — this is exactly the kind of indicator-mixing the convention warns about, so no new investigation was needed there. The wiki page (draft status, 7 citations, no TODOs) documents the stable-metropolitan-borders history (1814 Kiel treaty, 1814-1905 union, 1905 independence, 1940 occupation) consistently with this external knowledge, so it corroborates but is not the sole basis. No sub-territory fold-up risk (Norway is the reporting unit itself, not a component), no entrepot risk for FAO livestock/dairy production data. Territory was constant across the whole 1937-1951 span and equals the candidate's, so verified_equal applies.

The candidate NSW-1800-1900 is explicitly modeled (per its own draft wiki page, corroborated against CShapes 2.0's boundary-year sequencing) as the actual evolving Colony of New South Wales, whose area shrinks in discrete steps as Van Diemen's Land (1825), South Australia (1836), Victoria (1851) and Queensland (6 June 1859) were carved out. The assertion's observed span, 1854-1898, straddles the 1859 Queensland separation, i.e. a real mid-span territorial change to the reporting entity. Because sa_colonial is a contemporary South Australian colonial statistical register, its 'New South Wales' label almost certainly reports on whatever NSW's current administrative extent was in each publication year (the same evolving unit CShapes and the wiki describe), which is the correct match target -- there is no separate/larger union or federation scope issue here (unlike Sweden-Norway or Cisleithania cases) and no sub-territory fold-up (NSW is not a component being matched to a larger parent). I pulled the actual per-year wheat series from matched_rows.parquet for 1854-1898: it shows smooth, gradually rising output (786k bushels in 1854 growing irregularly to ~10.5M bushels by 1897) with NO visible level-shift or drop across the 1859 Queensland-separation boundary, consistent with Queensland's wheat output being negligible relative to NSW's rather than with any confusion of reporting scope. So the territory-label match is the best available one, but because the underlying colonial entity genuinely changed shape mid-span (1859 Queensland cession, inside 1854-1898), this cannot be verified_equal per the stated rule -- it is confirm/best_available.
verdict.wiki_note: The assertion's observed span (1854-1898) straddles the 1859 Queensland separation that this page already documents as a mid-life boundary change for NSW-1800-1900; the sa_colonial wheat series (1854-1898, pulled from matched_rows.parquet) shows no level-shift at 1859, suggesting Queensland's wheat output was negligible relative to NSW's rather than being folded into or double-counted with any Queensland series -- useful corroboration the page does not currently cite.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes 195 rows of "New Zealand" grain-production data (Wheat, Barley, Oats/"Oast", Maize) from a colonial statistical source (sa_colonial) for 1854-1898 to NZL-1840-2025. This entire observed span falls before the 1901 acquisitions of Cook Islands/Niue and the 1907 dominion transition, and well after the main-island territory (North/South/Stewart Islands) had stabilized in the 1860s per the wiki's own account (no cessions/annexations of the mainland). The wiki page (draft status) documents CShapes back-projection to 1840 with no territorial change through 1907 and beyond, and explicitly notes the Pacific-territory omission only becomes relevant post-1901/1926 — outside this span. The staple magnitudes (wheat median ~6.07M bushels, barley ~748k, oats ~9.8M bushels) are consistent in scale with 19th-century New Zealand colonial cereal agriculture (a temperate settler economy of a few hundred thousand people by the 1890s), not with any narrower sub-region or a combined/entrepot reporting scheme — grains are not the classic re-export commodity and there's no adjacent territory (Cook Islands, Niue) with grain-farming capacity at this scale. No combined-reporting risk (unlike Sweden-Norway or Yemen-type unions): New Zealand had no political union partner in this period. No sub-territory fold-up risk: "New Zealand" here plainly denotes the colony itself, not a component. Given the span is fully contained within a single stable territorial configuration (mainland NZ, no boundary changes, before any external territory administration began), confirm with verified_equal is appropriate.

review.basis: Territory reconstructed first: the Colony of New Zealand 1854-1898 comprised North, South and Stewart Islands plus the Chathams, with no cession and no metropolitan/union complication — it was never part of a wider union (unlike Sweden-Norway or Cisleithania cases) and acquired no productive dependency in this span (Cook Islands and Niue only in 1901, Western Samoa 1920, Tokelau 1926, all after the observed years, and correctly outside the label's scope). The only in-span territorial changes are the annexations of the uninhabited subantarctic Auckland/Campbell Islands (1863) and the Kermadecs (1887) — agriculturally null, but genuine annexations, so the reporting territory was not strictly constant across 1854-1898 and I record best_available rather than verified_equal. Fold-up (failure family 5) is the real risk here, since Canterbury alone held more than half of NZ's wheat land and could plausibly masquerade as "New Zealand": the magnitudes rule it out. NZ wheat acreage rose to ~250,000 acres by 1883 and ~400,000 by the 1890s; at colonial yields of ~25 bu/acre that is ~6-10M bushels, matching the observed median 6.07M bushels, whereas Canterbury-only would be roughly half that. Oats ("Oast") median 9.82M bushels and barley 748k bushels are likewise colony-scale for a territory whose oat acreage exceeded its wheat acreage by the 1890s; maize is a single trivial North Island observation, exactly as expected for a temperate colony. Entrepot risk is nil (these are domestic crop returns, not trade); combined reporting is nil (sa_colonial, the UK statistical abstract for colonial possessions, reports each colony as its own unit and carried Cook Islands separately under British Settlements Oceania until 1901); and there is no competing period split — NZL-1840-2025 is a single row covering the whole span, so no split_reroute basis exists. The candidate's 1907-vintaged CShapes polygon is a back-projection for this span, but mainland NZ geography is unchanged between 1898 and 1907, so the vintage introduces no scope error. Residual caveat, not a routing defect: colonial agricultural returns of this era under-enumerated Maori cultivation, so the series under-counts output within a territory that is nonetheless correctly identified.
review.wiki_note: Partial answer to oq-pre-1886-polygon: for crop data the pre-1886 extent is not a live problem — the only in-span territorial additions before 1898 were the uninhabited Auckland/Campbell Islands (1863) and Kermadecs (1887), with no arable land, so the back-projected polygon does not misstate the agricultural reporting territory for 1854-1898. Separate data-quality caveat worth recording: colonial-era NZ agricultural returns systematically under-enumerated Maori cultivation, so pre-1900 crop series under-count production within a correctly-scoped territory.

verdict.basis: The sa_colonial source's "South Australia" wheat/barley/oats/wine series (median 7.36M bushels wheat over 33 years) is agriculturally plausible only for South Australia's core arable belt (Adelaide Plains/Mid North/Riverland), not for any larger Australian aggregate — consistent with the candidate AUSA-1836-1900 being the standalone colony rather than the ~3x-larger AUS-1800-1901 aggregate that the wiki page explicitly says this record was created to avoid colliding with. However, South Australia administered the Northern Territory from 1863 to 1911 (documented in the page's own open question), so the colony's actual administered territory expanded partway through the observed 1854-1898 span. Agricultural crop output from NT desert territory would be negligible and doesn't distort the magnitudes, but strictly the reporting territory was not constant across the whole span, so this is best_available rather than verified_equal.

The assertion routes 195 rows labeled "Tasmania" (crop staples: wheat, barley, oats, potatoes, wine — bushels/gallons, 1854-1898) from source sa_colonial to TAS-1825-1900 (Van Diemen's Land/Tasmania, 1825-1900). Tasmania is an island whose land boundary is a coastline, not a negotiated border; it existed as a separate British colony continuously from its 1825 separation from NSW until 1900 federation, with no annexations, cessions, or internal territorial changes during that span. The wiki page (wiki_status draft, but substantively documented: CShapes 2.0 gwcode 906, 68,137 km² vs. modern land area ~68,401 km², 3 source citations) correctly identifies this as a stable, unchanging insular territory for the whole 1825-1900 window, and the observed data years (1854-1898) fall entirely within that stable span. Staple magnitudes (wheat ~930k bushels median) are plausible for a mid-19th-century island agricultural colony of this size and pose no red flag for combined-reporting, entrepot re-export, or sub-territory fold-up (Tasmania is a whole colony, not a component of one, and sa_colonial's other siblings — NSW, WA, SA, Victoria, Queensland — show it treats each Australasian colony as its own separately-reported unit, so there is no fold-up into a larger federation label here since the label is literally "Tasmania" itself). No boundary-vintage concern either: the coastline is invariant regardless of the CShapes 1886 vintage stamp. This is a clean, low-risk case: label territory = candidate territory = constant throughout the observed span.

The source label 'Victoria' under sa_colonial for 1854-1898 reports wheat/barley/oats/wine/maize crop output at magnitudes consistent with a whole agrarian colony (median wheat ~5.7M bushels/yr), not a sub-region or entrepot. The Colony of Victoria's borders were fixed at separation from NSW on 1 July 1851 and remained unchanged through federation in 1901 (well-established historical geography, corroborated by the wiki page and general knowledge of Australian colonial boundaries), so the reporting territory is constant across the entire 1854-1898 observed span and equals the candidate polity VIC-1851-1900's territory for that whole span. No union/empire scope issue (Victoria was never joined with another colony under one federal government pre-1901), no sub-territory fold-up (Victoria itself, not a district within it, is named), and no combined-reporting risk (single colony name, single administration). The wiki page is draft status but its territorial claim (fixed 1851 borders) reflects standard, independently verifiable Australian colonial history, not an idiosyncratic guess, so it is not being relied on circularly.

The assertion's label 'Western Australia' names the same self-governing colony as candidate AUWA-1829-1900 (1829-1900), which fully contains the observed span 1854-1898. Western Australia was a distinct British colony, not a sub-territory of a larger federal Australia label during this period (federation only occurred in 1901, after the observed span ends), so this is a direct name match rather than a sub-territory fold-up. The wiki page (draft status, 3 source citations) documents the colony's border with South Australia at the 129°E meridian as fixed since 1831 and unchanged, meaning the reporting territory stayed constant across the whole observed span 1854-1898 - no annexation, cession, or federation event intervened before 1898. Staple magnitudes (wheat ~311k bushels, barley ~72k bushels median) are plausible for a small colonial agricultural economy of WA's modest population in this era, with no unexplained scale that would suggest entrepot re-export or scope mismatch. The single polity in polities_database.csv for this name/ISO confirms there is no competing candidate to reroute to.

review.basis: I inspected the underlying source rows in /home/usuario/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.parquet: `sa_colonial` is a set of South Australian colonial statistical abstracts (source_detail SA_1854_1872 / SA_1869_1883 / SA_1883_1898, page-level tables) carrying comparative crop returns for exactly eight reporting units — New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia, Western Australia, Tasmania, Queensland, New Zealand, Cape of Good Hope — each with 195 rows. "Western Australia" is therefore a peer colony column in an inter-colonial comparison table, i.e. the Colony of Western Australia itself, not a district of South Australia and not a component folded into an Australian aggregate; the label is neither broader nor narrower than the candidate. The arithmetic corroborates this independently of any prose: WA wheat runs 170k–865k bushels (median 311k) while South Australia in the same table runs 3–14 million and Victoria 1.3–19.6 million. A figure two orders of magnitude below SA and Victoria is exactly what the sparsely settled Swan River colony implies (European population ~12k in 1854, ~160k by 1898, with cropping confined to the southwest); it is flatly incompatible with any reading of the label as a mainland aggregate, and equally incompatible with a within-SA district (SA's own column is reported separately and is 20–40x larger). The series is smooth and monotone-with-weather across the whole 1854–1898 span, rising to 865k bushels in 1898 with the gold-rush population surge — no step that would signal a scope change, and no combined-reporting artefact. Boundary vintage is a non-issue here: Western Australia's eastern boundary was fixed at the 129°E meridian from the colony's foundation era (1829/1831 proclamations) and did not move at any point in the observed span or in the candidate's 1829–1900 period, so the reporting territory equals the candidate's territory AND is constant throughout — hence verified_equal rather than best_available. The draft wiki page (3.6 KB, 3 citations, all Wikipedia) states the same 129°E constancy and the 1901 federation cut-off; it agrees with, but did not drive, this conclusion. Pre-1870 WA cells are blank/NaN in the source (returns simply not carried in the earliest abstract), which is a coverage gap, not evidence of a different scope.

source_convention.convention: sa_colonial rows carry indicator='yield', but the values are TOTAL colony production for the year (Bushels for grains, Gallons for wine), not per-acre yields. Treat them as production series.
source_convention.evidence: Values in the source tables run to millions of Bushels per colony-year (e.g. Victoria wheat 19.6m in 1898, South Australia 14.6m in 1883); a per-acre yield would be ~10-20 bushels. Nineteenth-century colonial abstracts use 'yield' in the sense of total produce.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes Mitchell's "el salvador" 1894-1960 series (192 rows: cotton lint/seed, sugar, beer, cattle, poultry etc.) to SLV-1821-2025 via ISO match. El Salvador has been a single continuously-bounded national reporting unit since 1821 independence; there is no union/empire, no combined-reporting partner, and no sub-territory fold-up risk (the country itself, not a province, is the reporting unit). The wiki page (draft status, but substantive: 5868 bytes, 5 source citations, no TODOs) documents the one relevant territorial change in the full 1821-2025 span -- the 1992 ICJ ruling ceding ~330 km2 to Honduras -- and explicitly shows the observed data span (1894-1960) falls entirely within the 1884-1992 sub-period during which the boundary was fixed by the 1884 Jutiapa Agreement and unaffected by the later ICJ transfer. So territory was constant across the whole 1894-1960 observed span. Magnitudes (cotton lint 20,000 ha, sugar 18,500 t, poultry 1.89M head) are plausible for a 21,000 km2 Central American agrarian economy of the era and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change. No entrepot/re-export risk (El Salvador is not a transit hub) and no evidence of combined reporting with a neighbor. I treat the draft page's factual claims about the Jutiapa Agreement and ICJ ruling as independently verifiable historical facts (well-documented international law/history, consistent with general encyclopedic knowledge) rather than relying on the page's routing conclusion alone -- the routing conclusion itself is trivial here since El Salvador the nation-state is exactly the reporting territory Mitchell's compilation covers.

Mauritius was a stable British Crown Colony (island of Mauritius plus small administrative dependencies: Rodrigues, Agalega, Cargados Carajos, and the Chagos Archipelago) throughout the observed span 1909-1945, with no annexation, cession, or boundary change during this period — British rule ran continuously from 1810 until independence in 1968, well after the span ends. The IIA "Mauritius" label in this period denotes the same administrative unit as the candidate polity MUS-1800-2025. Staple magnitudes strongly corroborate this: sugar raw centrifugal at a median ~235,000 tonnes/year is exactly the scale expected for Mauritius, historically one of the world's leading sugarcane-export colonies (sugar was ~90% of exports per the wiki's cited source), while tea (median 45 ha), coffee (median 7 ha), tobacco (median 300 tonnes) and groundnuts (median 100 tonnes) are all plausible smallholder/minor-crop scales for a small island economy, not a larger regional aggregate. No evidence of double-reporting, entrepot re-export distortion, or sub-territory fold-up — Mauritius itself is the reporting unit, not a component of a larger polity. The wiki page (draft status, 3 source citations) documents the same stable-territory history but is not relied on as the sole evidence; the magnitude plausibility check independently supports the match. The only open question on the page concerns whether the Chagos Archipelago is included in the WHEP polygon, which is a polygon-definition question, not a reporting-territory discontinuity during 1909-1945, and does not affect the confirm verdict.

Assertion denmark|fao1952|1937-1951 routes FAO 1952 yearbook's "Denmark" label to DNK-1920-2025 for years 1937-1951. The candidate's wiki page (reviewed, 5 source citations) documents metropolitan Denmark (Jutland, Zealand, Funen, Northern Schleswig, ~43,000 km²) as territorially stable from the 1920 Schleswig plebiscite through the present, explicitly noting the 1940-1945 German occupation caused no permanent territorial change and hence no WHEP split. The observed span 1937-1951 straddles that occupation but lies entirely within this single stable-border period, so there is no annexation/cession/union-scope issue analogous to Sweden-Norway or Austria-Cisleithania to worry about here — Denmark was never part of a union in this era and the source label is unambiguous. Staple magnitudes (meat ~242k tonnes, poultry ~397k thousand heads) are consistent with Denmark's well-known dairy/bacon/meat export economy of the period. The population figure (median 540k) initially looks too low for Denmark's ~3.8-4.3M actual population, but the bundle's own source_conventions entry (verified 2026-08-14) already resolves this: the FAO 1952 population item code conflates five indicators (total, agricultural, agricultural-occupied, and sex splits) under one code, and a figure around a third of total population is the agricultural-occupied indicator, not a defect or territorial mismatch — this is a previously-established convention, not new territory evidence, so I treat it as confirmed background rather than a fresh finding. No sub-territory fold-up, entrepot, or combined-reporting pattern applies to a "Denmark" label at this scale. Verdict: confirm, verified_equal, since the reporting territory equals the candidate's and was constant across the whole 1937-1951 span.

The assertion routes 190 rows of FAO/Juan agricultural data labeled "paraguay" (iso=pry) for 1911-1931 to PRY-1870-1932 by ISO+year containment. The candidate's period (1870-1932) fully contains the observed span, and Paraguay's actual governed/administered territory was stable throughout 1870-1932 (post-Triple-Alliance treaties settled with Brazil/Argentina by 1872; the Chaco Boreal dispute with Bolivia was unresolved but produced no change in effective administration until the 1935 armistice/1938 arbitration, both after our span ends in 1931). Staple magnitudes (maize ~31,810t, tobacco ~9,587t, seed cotton ~8,217t, sugar cane ~10,230ha) are plausible for Paraguay's populated eastern agricultural zone and show no discontinuity flagged in neighbor_segments (next split at 1932 = Chaco War outbreak, outside this span). The wiki page (draft status, 0 source_citations, but with a well-documented and previously verified polygon-caveat addendum from 2026-07-24/08-14) already discloses that the attached CShapes polygon overstates territory by ~87% because it includes the disputed, sparsely-populated Chaco Boreal — but that is a POLYGON measurement issue, not a reporting-territory issue: agricultural production data is concentrated in the settled eastern region actually administered by Paraguay throughout the period, so the data-routing match holds. No annexation/cession affecting Paraguay's own reporting territory occurred within 1911-1931, so the span is internally constant.

review.basis: The label is the bare national name "paraguay" with iso "pry" for 1911-1931, routed to PRY-1870-1932 (1870-1932). None of the standard scope failures apply: Paraguay in this era was a unitary republic with no colonies, no union partner, no federated components, and no second polity that could be folded into the same label (unlike Yemen/Sweden-Norway/Austria cases), and there is no sub-territory fold-up risk — "paraguay" is not a province, island or district of a larger candidate. Nor is there an entrepot concern: the staple mix (tobacco 9,587 t, maize 31,810 t, seed cotton 8,217 t, sugar cane 10,230 ha, paddy 900 t) is exactly the agronomic profile of subtropical eastern Paraguay at a population of roughly 0.8-1.0 million, small-country scale, with no commodity the territory could not itself grow. Boundary vintage is also clean for the years in question: Paraguay's de jure limits were fixed by the post-Triple-Alliance treaties (Brazil 1872, Argentina 1876 plus the 1878 Hayes award) and did not formally change again until the 1938 Chaco arbitration, so 1911-1931 sits wholly inside one stable legal boundary and inside the candidate span, with the neighbour segments (PRY-1932-1938, PRY-1938-2025) beginning only after the observed data end. I mark best_available rather than verified_equal for two reasons that are about the candidate's territorial encoding, not the routing. First, the candidate is internally inconsistent about what its territory is: the CSV/front-matter states 157,000 km2 while the attached CShapes gwcode-150 geometry measures roughly 293,507 km2 (+87%), the difference being the Chaco Boreal. Second, during the observed span effective control of that Chaco was not constant — Bolivian fortines advanced into it through the 1910s and 1920s ahead of the 1932 war — so no single fixed polygon equals the territory across 1911-1931. This does not damage the match, because Paraguayan agricultural statistics of the period were compiled from the settled Region Oriental, which the 157,000 km2 figure approximates; the disputed Chaco contributed essentially nothing to these crop and livestock series. The candidate is therefore the correct and best available polity, with a known territorial-encoding imprecision that falls outside the data-bearing area. Note on evidence honesty: I read the wiki page (draft, 3,323 bytes, zero counted source citations), but the territorial facts I relied on — the treaty settlement, the unresolved Chaco dispute, and the concentration of agriculture in the east — are standard history I hold independently, and the magnitude plausibility check comes from the bundle's own data, not from the page.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes 190 rows of "Queensland" agricultural production (wheat, barley, oats, maize, wine) 1859-1898 from source "sa_colonial" to candidate QUE-1859-1900, the Colony of Queensland (separated from NSW 6 June 1859, federated into Australia 1 Jan 1901). The wiki page (draft status, 2 source citations, no todo markers) documents Queensland as a distinct self-governing British colony for this whole span, separated from NSW in 1859 and persisting unchanged until 1900/1901 federation — a well-established, stable colonial-era territory with clear historical record independent of the page's own drafting. The observed span (1859-1898) falls entirely within the candidate's period (1859-1900) and matches the colony's actual constant existence — no annexation/cession/union affecting the reporting unit itself occurred in this window (the Torres Strait Islands annexation 1872/1879 and the BNG protectorate 1883-1902 are noted in the wiki as administrative additions that did not materially expand Queensland's own agricultural producing territory — BNG was never a source of wheat/barley/maize output, and the page itself flags BNG as excluded from the polygon/production territory). Staple magnitudes (wheat ~134k bushels, maize ~1.39M bushels median) are plausible for a single mid-sized settler colony's agricultural output, not for all of Australia or a larger union, supporting that "Queensland" here means the colony itself, not a broader Australian aggregate — ruling out the union/empire-scope failure mode. No sub-territory fold-up concern: Queensland is the reporting unit itself, not a component being folded into a larger parent. This is a clean case of a distinct, stably-bounded colonial polity being labeled by its own name in a colonial-era statistical source (South Australian colonial statistics register, "sa_colonial", covering fellow Australasian colonies) — territory equals candidate and stayed constant across the whole observed span.

The observed span 1913-1917 falls entirely inside candidate BGR-1913-1918's period 1913-1918, a stable interval bounded by two undisputed treaty events (Treaty of Bucharest, 10 Aug 1913 at the start; armistice 29 Sep 1918 after the observed span ends). No territorial change occurred to Bulgaria's sovereign borders during 1913-1917 itself: Bulgaria joined the Central Powers in Oct 1915 and briefly administered occupied Serbian/Romanian territory during the war, but this was wartime military occupation, not a change to Bulgaria's own reporting territory, and Bulgaria's own agricultural statistics (barley, tobacco, sugar beet, cotton) would be reported for Bulgaria proper, not occupied zones. The staple magnitudes (barley ~240k ha, tobacco ~15k ha, sugar beet ~45k ha) are plausible for a ~96,000-110,000 km2 Balkan agrarian state and show no discontinuity against the neighbor segments BGR-1878-1913 (pre-Balkan-Wars, larger territory) or BGR-1918-1919 (post-WWI), consistent with a single stable reporting territory for the whole 1913-1917 span.
