The wiki page is draft status (unreviewed) so its claims are not independent evidence, but its territorial narrative (post-Balkan-Wars reduced Bulgaria, ~96,000 km2, losses of Southern Dobruja and Macedonia) is corroborated by well-known Balkan history (Treaty of Bucharest 1913) independent of the page itself. No sub-territory fold-up, entrepot, or combined-reporting risk applies here -- 'Bulgaria' is a straightforward national label matching a national-scope candidate for its entire observed span.

The assertion routes IIA "china, mainland" 1932-1944 to CHN-1932-1945 (China proper excluding Manchukuo/Manchuria, 6,710,264 km2). The candidate's wiki (draft status, 9928 bytes, treated as unreviewed hypothesis) documents a specific, checkable reasoning chain: China proper (22 provinces) explicitly excludes the three Manchurian provinces administered as Manchukuo from 1932; a prior open question (oq-flax...) was already audited and closed with corrected figures; and a 2026-06-29 decision explicitly rejected splitting at 1937 (Sino-Japanese War outbreak) after checking staple magnitudes (rice ~46.7M t, wheat ~10.97M t) against China-proper-scale national totals, concluding the FAO/IIA reporting basis stayed geographically consistent (China proper excl. Manchukuo) even though administrative control fragmented after 1937. Independently, the bundle's own staple_magnitudes (soybeans median 5.27M t, sesame 419,700 t, rapeseed 2.48M t, cotton lint/seed in the 1.5-2.3M ha range) are plausible for interwar China-proper agricultural output at this scale (national soybean output of that era ran roughly 10-11M t with a large Manchurian share, so ~5.3M t for the non-Manchurian remainder is consistent) and the neighbor_segments show smooth adjacency to CHN-1921-1932 and CHN-1945-1947 with no magnitude discontinuity flagged. The observed span (1932-1944) sits entirely inside the candidate's declared period (1932-1945) and, per the wiki's own reasoning, the reporting territory (geographic China proper excl. Manchukuo) did not change within that span — only political control did, which the source's own compilers did not use as their reporting boundary. No sub-territory fold-up, entrepot, or combined-reporting pattern applies here (China proper is the reporting unit itself, not a component folded into a larger one). I did not find anything in the page that looks wrong; the source_citations=0 metadata is a metadata/parser artifact given the page visibly cites biger-1995 and FAO 1952 documentation inline, so I do not treat the page as inadequate, but I do treat its claims as a hypothesis corroborated here mainly by internal magnitude plausibility rather than a fresh external source I personally verified.

Guadeloupe 1909-1945 assertion routes IIA sugar/cacao/coffee/cotton data (187 rows, 33 distinct years) to GLP-1816-2025. Guadeloupe was a stable French colony throughout this entire span — no annexation, cession, or administrative territorial change occurred between 1909 and 1945 (the DOM transition was 1946, after the observed span ends; the Saint-Barthélemy/Saint-Martin separation was 2007, over 60 years later). The commodities reported (sugar, cacao, coffee, cotton) are all crops genuinely grown on Guadeloupe's own soil — this is a small (1,652 km²) sugar-and-tropical-crop island colony, not a transit/entrepôt port, so there is no re-export inflation risk. Magnitudes are plausible for the island's size: sugar median ~37,500 tonnes/yr fits Guadeloupe's historical sugar-cane economy; coffee/cacao at ~1,000 tonnes and cotton at 25 ha are modest, consistent with minor secondary crops on a small island. The wiki page (draft status, 0 source citations) documents the same territory/history but is itself unreviewed and thin, so I did not rely on it as proof — I corroborated independently via known colonial history (no territorial event in this specific 1909-1945 window) and via magnitude plausibility for an island of this size producing these crops. Since the reporting territory equals the candidate's territory and it did not change anywhere within the observed 1909-1945 span, this is a verified_equal confirm, not merely best_available.

review.basis: Territory first: across 1909-1945 the reporting territory was the French colony "Guadeloupe et dépendances" — Basse-Terre/Grande-Terre plus Marie-Galante, Les Saintes, La Désirade, Saint-Barthélemy and the northern part of Saint-Martin — with no annexation, cession or separation; the 1940-43 Vichy interlude under Admiral Robert and the 1946 colony-to-DOM change (after the span) altered status, not territory, and the St-Barthélemy/Saint-Martin detachment is 2007, far outside the span. So no split is warranted and GLP-1816-2025 is the only WHEP row covering these years (MAF-2007-2025 begins in 2007). Scope/aggregation checked against the data: I read the 187 IIA rows in ~/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.csv. Sugar raw centrifugal 38,523 t (1909-13 avg) and 37,493 t (1910); coffee green 500-1,100 t; cacao 600-1,200 t; cotton a few hundred ha and tens of tonnes. Those are island-Guadeloupe magnitudes on ~1,650 km², and Martinique is reported separately at comparable size (38,811 t sugar 1909-13), so the "french antilles:" prefix in the raw labels is a yearbook grouping heading, not a two-colony aggregate — combined reporting ruled out. Continuity is smooth in sugar/coffee/cacao with no step; the interwar decline (cacao 900 t -> 100-200 t, coffee to 300-400 t) is the well-known collapse of Guadeloupe's secondary export crops toward sugar/banana monoculture, not a scope change. Why best_available rather than verified_equal: pipelines/polity-autoimprove/state/iia_label_provenance.csv shows the layer-B label "guadeloupe" is assembled from three raw IIA labels — "french antilles: guadeloupe" (dominant, 0.78), "french antilles: guadeloupe and dependencies" (union 93%) and "french antilles: guadeloupe: marie-galante" — i.e. a whole plus narrower variants of itself, differing by roughly 200 km² (~13%) of dependency territory, with territory_signal recorded as "mixed". A label with no single reporting territory cannot be asserted equal to the polity's, even though every variant sits inside GLP and no better-granularity WHEP row exists. The wiki page is a draft with zero source citations; I used it only for the polygon/period narrative and reached the territorial history independently.
review.wiki_note: IIA (1909-1945) routes to this row through a layer-B label assembled from three raw yearbook labels — "french antilles: guadeloupe", "...guadeloupe and dependencies" and "...guadeloupe: marie-galante" — so individual cells may be Guadeloupe proper (~1,438 km²), the colony with its dependencies (~1,700 km²), or Marie-Galante alone; layer B keeps one row per cell with no trace of which, so the series is best_available, not an exact-territory match. Data-quality defect: IIA "cotton seed" for 1934 is 3,884,800 tonnes against 0-120 t in every neighbouring year (and 0 ha sown that year) — an ingestion/OCR error of roughly 10^4-10^5 that should be dropped before any aggregation.

source_convention.convention: In the IIA yearbooks the "French Antilles: X" heading names the individual colony, not an Antilles-wide aggregate; each colony is tabulated separately.
source_convention.evidence: Layer-B IIA rows report Guadeloupe sugar raw centrifugal at 38,523 t (1909-13) and Martinique separately at 38,811 t (1909-13) and 41,327 t (1925-29); an aggregate under either label would be roughly the sum, and French Guiana appears as its own label at ~100 t.

verdict.basis: The wiki (reviewed, 45 source citations) documents Luxembourg's borders as static since the 1839/1867 settlement, with Biger explicitly stating "since 1867 no changes in the boundary line were made" and noting the two German occupations (1914-18, 1940-44) did not alter territory. The FAO1952 label is "Luxembourg" specifically (not "Belgium-Luxembourg"), and the reported staple magnitudes (poultry median 4k heads, meat median 11k tonnes, rye 9k ha) are consistent with Luxembourg's small size, not the much larger Belgium-Luxembourg aggregate (BLX-1850-1999) the wiki notes exists separately for FAOSTAT purposes — this independently corroborates the source is reporting the standalone Grand Duchy, not a combined entity. The 1937-1951 span includes the 1940-1944 German occupation, an administrative disruption named in the routing guidance as a disqualifier for verified_equal even though it did not change the recognized international boundary, so I mark best_available rather than verified_equal out of caution for that occupation interval.

The observed span (1909-1945) lies entirely inside the colonial period 1886-1954 assigned to SUR-1886-1954 (Dutch Guiana), after both the 1899 Paris arbitration and 1906 Brazil-Surinam boundary settlement, and well before the 1954 charter granting autonomy. IIA "suriname" data (coffee, cacao, sugar, oranges, tobacco) is single-territory colonial reporting with no plausible union/combined-reporting or sub-territory issue for a small stand-alone Dutch colony. Magnitudes are modest and plausible for the colony's scale and show no evident step-change suggesting a scope shift within the span. The wiki page is draft with 0 source citations, so its narrative was treated as hypothesis; corroboration instead comes from externally-verifiable facts (CShapes 2.0's three stable, identically-sized COW-115 features; the well-documented 1899/1906 boundary settlements predating the data) rather than the page itself.

The assertion covers FAO 1952 yearbook rows labeled 'Tunisia' for 1937-1951 (crops/livestock: broad beans, chick peas, oats, cattle, camels, buffaloes, meat, horses/mules/asses). Tunisia was a French protectorate over this entire span (established 1881, independence only in 1956), with no annexation, cession, or boundary change between 1937 and 1951 -- CShapes confirms identical territory (~164,000 km2, COW 616) across three vintage entries spanning 1886-2019, i.e. constant through this narrow 15-year observed window. The reported magnitudes are plausible for Tunisia's actual size and population (~2.6-2.8M in this era): oats 25k ha, broad beans 39k ha, chick peas 8k ha, meat 18k tonnes, horses/mules/asses 72k head -- all consistent with a country of this scale, not a larger union or a sub-territory. There is no union/empire-scope ambiguity (unlike Sweden-Norway or Austria-Cisleithania cases) since French Tunisia was administered as a distinct protectorate, not folded into metropolitan France's own statistics the way Algeria was. The already-verified source_convention for fao1952 (five population indicators sharing one item code) is orthogonal to this crop/livestock assertion but confirms fao1952 is a well-behaved, per-country-labeled source in this period, supporting confirm here too. Reporting territory equals the candidate's for the whole observed span and stayed constant, so verified_equal applies.

The Mitchell "guadeloupe" label (ISO glp) reports on the French Caribbean island archipelago, which was continuously French sovereign territory (colony, then DOM from 1946) across the entire 1850-1960 observed span, with no annexation, cession, or administrative separation occurring in that window (the only administrative change, separation of Saint-Barthélemy/Saint-Martin, happened in 2007, outside the span). The staple magnitudes (sugar cane ~22,000 ha, raw centrifugal sugar ~39,500 t, bananas ~109,000 t median) are entirely plausible for a 1,652 km2 tropical island economy and show no discontinuity consistent with a territorial scope change. This is a direct ISO/name match with no sub-territory fold-up or union-scope ambiguity (unlike Sweden-Norway or Cisleithania cases) and no entrepot/re-export concern since sugar and bananas are genuinely grown on Guadeloupe itself.

review.basis: Numbers first: sugar raw centrifugal median 39,500 t (n=104), cane area median 22,000 ha (n=65), bananas median 109,000 t (n=14) on a 1,652 km2 (165,200 ha) archipelago. 22,000 ha of cane is ~13% of total land area — high but exactly what a monoculture sugar island implies (independent source: cane occupied 59% of cultivated land in 1856, 45% in 1895, 66% in 1939), and it is bounded by the island's size, so the label cannot be a larger territory. The sugar level is the decisive test: Guadeloupe alone made 42,000 t at its 1835 colonial peak, so a 104-year median of 39,500 t sits squarely on Guadeloupe-only output; a combined "French Antilles" label (Guadeloupe + Martinique, MTQ-1816-2025, 1,234 km2) would run roughly double, and any French-empire or metropolitan scope would be an order of magnitude larger. Bananas ~109,000 t in the post-1946 years matches Guadeloupe's known mid-century export scale for a DOM of this size. So the arithmetic independently implies a single ~1,600 km2 Lesser Antilles cane-and-banana island — the candidate's scope. Failure families cleared: no union/empire fold-out (Mitchell's Americas tables report French Caribbean colonies individually, and ISO in the data is GLP); no sub-territory fold-up (the label is the whole colony, not Marie-Galante/Basse-Terre/a district); no entrepot risk (cane and bananas are grown on the island, not transshipped); no combined reporting; no boundary-vintage issue for a physically invariant island; and no period splits in our DB — GLP is one continuous 1816-2025 row, so magnitude continuity across splits is not at stake. Not verified_equal, however: the reporting territory did not stay constant across 1850-1960. Saint-Barthelemy was Swedish until the retrocession treaty and was attached to Guadeloupe on 16 March 1878, so pre-1878 "Guadeloupe" is ~21 km2 (1.3%) smaller than the candidate's polygon; the 1886 CShapes vintage carries the post-1878 extent back over 1850-1877. The agronomic effect is negligible (St-Barthelemy is arid and grew essentially no cane), so the routing is the best available and the data are unaffected in practice — but a mid-span annexation means no single polity equals the reporting territory throughout, hence best_available.
review.wiki_note: The Summary asserts the archipelago "comprising ... Saint-Barthelemy" has "been under continuous French sovereignty since 1816" and the polygon section claims a pre-1886 back-projection introduces "< 5 km2 (< 0.3%)" difference with "no territorial difference expected for islands". Both are wrong: Saint-Barthelemy was a Swedish colony from 1784 and was retroceded to France and attached to Guadeloupe only on 16 March 1878, so for 1816-1877 the GLP territory was ~21 km2 (1.3%) smaller than the CShapes 1886 polygon. Open question oq-glp-pre-1886-cshapes should be closed with this answer rather than the expected "none". Data impact is negligible — Saint-Barthelemy produced essentially no cane or bananas — but the Mitchell 1850-1960 series therefore spans a territorial change and cannot be verified_equal.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes 181 rows of "mauritius" sugar cane data (1856-1960, median 108,000 tonnes) from Mitchell to MUS-1800-2025 by ISO code. Mauritius was a single British colony throughout this entire span (annexed 1810, independence not until 1968), with no boundary changes, partitions, or territorial disputes affecting the main island during 1856-1960. Sugar cane is exactly the commodity historically dominant in Mauritius's economy (the wiki page itself, citing Biger 1995, notes sugarcane accounted for ~90% of exports and 70% of labor force), so the magnitude and commodity are agronomically consistent with the island's known economic history — this is external corroboration, not reliance on the draft page's routing claim. The wiki page is thin (draft status, only 3 citations) but its core territorial claim — a small island with a stable coastline boundary and no boundary-moving events between 1800 and 2025 — is well-established general history and not contradicted by anything. The only open question (Chagos Archipelago status) does not affect this verdict: Chagos was never a sugar-producing territory and Mitchell's "Mauritius" sugar series plausibly reports only the main island's output, which is what the CShapes polygon covers. No annexation/cession/separation affected mainland Mauritius during 1856-1960, so the reporting territory was constant across the whole span.

Assertion routes FAO1952's 'Belgian Congo' label (180 rows, 1937-1951) to COD-1910-1960, the colonial polity spanning 1910-1960. Checked the known failure families: (a) combined reporting — inspected consolidated_layer_b.parquet directly and confirmed FAO1952 reports 'Belgian Congo' and 'Ruanda-Urundi'/'Ruanda Urundi' as three DISTINCT country labels, none sharing a polity_code, so this is not a combined Belgian-Congo-plus-Ruanda-Urundi label; (b) boundary vintage/annexation — Belgian Congo's external borders were fixed by pre-1910 bilateral treaties (France, Portugal, UK) and unchanged through independence in 1960, so the observed 1937-1951 span sits entirely within a territorially static period; (c) magnitude continuity — pulled Belgian Congo's cassava area/production series directly from the parquet (e.g. cassava production 5472/6250/6203 thousand tonnes and area 650/721/724 thousand ha in 1949/1950/1951) and found smooth continuity with no step suggesting a territorial change; (d) sub-territory fold-up — 'Belgian Congo' is the full colony-level label, not a sub-component like Katanga, matching the candidate's full-colony scope; (e) entrepot risk — commodities present (cassava, cotton, cacao, bananas, rice, cattle, sweet potatoes) are all agro-climatically plausible for Congo itself, not transit goods. The candidate's draft wiki page documents the same territorial-stability claim citing Biger 1995 (external source, 6 citations); I corroborated it independently via the parquet label-separation and magnitude checks rather than relying on the page's own decision log alone.

Assertion routes IIA "mexico" agricultural data (cotton, cacao, coffee, beans, flax) 1910-1945 to MEX-1848-2025. This candidate covers post-Mexican Cession/Gadsden Purchase Mexico with stable ~1.96M km2 territory from 1854 through at least 1960 (Chamizal, a trivial Rio Grande adjustment, occurred in 1960s, well after the observed span). The 1910-1945 window falls entirely inside this stable-borders period, spanning the Porfiriato's end, the Mexican Revolution, and into WWII, none of which altered Mexico's international boundaries per the wiki and the underlying Biger (1995) source (verified by reading the source file directly: p.381-383 confirms area 1,957,455 km2 and cession history). Reported crops (cotton, cacao, coffee, beans, castor beans) are all agronomically plausible for Mexico's diverse climate zones and match its well-known historical export profile — no entrepot or fold-up red flags. The wiki page, despite draft status, has 8 citations to a verifiable external source (Biger 1995) which I independently checked in wiki/sources/biger-1995.md and found genuine, not fabricated — so this is not circular reliance on an unreviewed page alone.

The observed span (1909-1945) falls entirely within Fiji's colonial period (British Crown Colony from 1874, independence not until 1970), during which the archipelago's extent was unchanged — Biger (1995) states Fiji 'has no land boundaries' and records no boundary event in this window, and the wiki independently corroborates area via GADM (18,649 km2) vs Biger's stated 18,325 km2 (1.8% agreement). This is a single-territory island colony, not a union/empire label, so there is no scope-fold-up or combined-reporting risk (Rotuma is flagged as a documented but immaterial 0.25%-of-area open question, already noted in the page). Staple magnitudes for 1909-1945 (sugar median ~92,906 t, tea/tobacco/cotton in small ha figures) are consistent with a small island economy dominated by sugar and copra exports, with no discontinuities suggesting a scope change across the span. Since the territory is constant for the entire 1909-1945 window (no annexation/cession/occupation inside it), verified_equal is appropriate despite the page being wiki_status draft, because the key territorial claims (no land boundary, no boundary events, area cross-check against an independent source) are corroborated externally via Biger-1995 rather than resting solely on the draft page's own assertions.

review.basis: The IIA label is the Colony of Fiji, and I established that from the source side first: pipelines/polity-autoimprove/state/iia_label_provenance.csv records the yearbook label "fiji islands" resolving one-to-one ("british fiji islands 100%") with no competing or component labels, and pipelines/polity-autoimprove/state/iia_territorial_notes.csv carries NO territorial/boundary-vintage note for Fiji (it does carry them for the genuinely tricky units — Egypt+Sudan, Japan/Korea/Taiwan, Dutch East Indies/Java-and-Madura, 1937 vs 1945 boundary totals), so the IIA compilers saw nothing scope-ambiguous here. Checked all five failure families explicitly: (1) no union/empire fold-up — the Colony of Fiji is not the Western Pacific High Commission, and IIA lists other WPHC territories (Gilbert & Ellice, Solomons, Tonga) as their own labels rather than inside Fiji; (2) no boundary vintage issue — an archipelago with no land frontier had no boundary event in 1909-1945 (Rotuma annexed 1881, cession 1874, independence 1970 all outside the span), so the reporting territory is CONSTANT across the whole observed span; (3) no combined reporting; (4) our single 1800-2025 row is not mis-split for this source's basis; (5) sub-territory fold-up ruled out — the label names the whole island group, not Viti Levu, Vanua Levu or a single mill district. Magnitudes corroborate independently: sugar raw centrifugal median 92,906 t is the right order for interwar CSR-era Fiji (rising to ~330k t by the FAOSTAT 1961 baseline), while tobacco 45 ha, tea 80 ha, cotton lint 4 ha and cacao 13 ha are token plantings appropriate to an 18,600 km² colony — i.e. production consistent with the land, not an entrepot/re-export signature (Fiji handled no plausible foreign sugar re-export at this scale). The draft wiki page's territorial claims (18,649 km² GADM vs Biger 18,325 km², "no land boundaries", no boundary event in span) are consistent with this but are not what the verdict rests on.
review.wiki_note: Answers open question oq-fji-rotuma-reporting-scope for the IIA source at least: iia_label_provenance.csv shows the yearbook label "fiji islands" resolving one-to-one to british fiji islands with no separate Rotuma line anywhere in the IIA label inventory, and iia_territorial_notes.csv records no territorial note for Fiji — so IIA's "Fiji" is the undivided colony and no Rotuma-scope adjustment is needed for these 178 rows.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes Mitchell's plain "ghana" label (ISO match, years 1898-1956) to GHA-1898-1957, the British Gold Coast colony in its 1898-expanded configuration (post-Ashanti/Northern-Territories incorporation) through the 1957 independence boundary. The candidate's period (1898-1957) fully contains the observed span (1898-1956), so no period-boundary misalignment. Neighbor segments show smooth cacao-bean magnitude progression (150t in 1896-97 under GHA-1888-1898 -> median 210,000t in 1898-1956 under this candidate -> median 259,000t in 1957-60 under GHA-1957-2025), consistent with Ghana's well-documented organic growth into the world's leading cocoa producer across this period, with no discontinuous jump at the 1957 transition that would signal a sudden change in reporting scope (e.g. Togoland being folded in abruptly). The candidate's own wiki page (draft status, but with 6 source citations to Biger-1995 and CShapes boundary data) documents that the Gold Coast Colony proper (CShapes polygon, 238,533 km²) excludes British Togoland (~33,773 km², ~14% of combined area) even though Togoland was administered as an integral part of the Gold Coast from 1920 (unified budget/customs) until the 1956 plebiscite/1957 formal incorporation. An earlier verification already accepted this same ~14% territorial understatement as tolerable for FAO's explicitly combined "Gold Coast and British Togoland" label covering 1949-1951 (a subset of this Mitchell span). Since Mitchell's plain "Ghana" label for the colonial period most plausibly derives from similar official Gold Coast government statistics (which would reflect the same unified administrative/customs treatment of Togoland from 1920), the same accepted approximation logic extends here, though I have not independently confirmed Mitchell's own territorial scope convention from a Mitchell source file. Given the territory never exactly equals the candidate's narrower CShapes polygon (constant ~14% understatement throughout, not a mid-span change), this is best_available rather than verified_equal.

The candidate HUN-1940-1944 (152,423 km², proxy polygon, Trianon+First Vienna Award+Second Vienna Award Transylvania, per its thorough draft wiki page) is the only existing polity covering 1940-1943 and is the historically correct de jure/de facto polity for the span. But direct inspection of the underlying whep_crops (juan) parquet for HUN barley/maize/rye area 1935-1948 shows NO step at the 1940 Second Vienna Award boundary (barley 444k→410k ha, maize 1,174k→1,146k ha, rye 622k→541k ha, 1939→1940) despite the award adding ~43,700 km² (≈40% more land) — the series instead runs smoothly through 1938-1944 at levels indistinguishable from the pre-annexation Trianon+First-Vienna-Award baseline (HUN-1938-1940's own 1938-39 figures). This matches an already-established convention of the same 'juan' source for other WWII-era European countries: pipelines/polity-autoimprove/11_retest_conventions.py's check_juan_finland and check_juan_czechoslovakia both verify that 'juan' reports a CONSTANT pre-war/pre-annexation territorial basis through wartime border changes (Finland's reduced 1940 borders held constant through the Karelia reconquest 1941-44; Czechoslovakia's pre-Munich basis held constant through the 1938 partition and 1945 restoration). Hungary now reproduces the same signature: the source appears to keep reporting on the smaller, pre-Second-Vienna-Award territory throughout 1940-1943, not the expanded candidate's actual territory. The candidate's own territory also changed mid-span (April 1941 Bačka/Baranja occupation added ~10,000 km² partway through the observed 1940-1943 window), which independently rules out verified_equal. No better existing polity exists for this span (HUN-1938-1940 ends in 1940, not 1943), so HUN-1940-1944 remains the best available routing target despite the apparent reporting-territory mismatch.
verdict.wiki_note: Direct inspection of whep_crops (juan) HUN barley/maize/rye hectares 1935-1948 shows no upward step at the 1940 Second Vienna Award boundary (e.g. maize 1,174,000 ha in 1939 vs 1,146,000 ha in 1940, despite ~43,700 km² / ~40% more land nominally added) — the series is statistically indistinguishable from the pre-annexation Trianon+First-Vienna-Award baseline through the whole 1940-1943 span. This firms up the page's own hedged "Data magnitude note" with concrete figures, and matches an established pattern already coded for the same source elsewhere (pipelines/polity-autoimprove/11_retest_conventions.py's check_juan_finland and check_juan_czechoslovakia), which verify that 'juan' reports on a constant pre-war territorial basis through wartime border changes for other WWII European countries. Likely implication: whep_crops/juan HUN figures for 1940-1944 probably reflect Trianon+First-Vienna-Award territory (~108,785 km²), not the full wartime-expanded ~152,000-172,000 km², so users should not treat this label's magnitudes as representative of the enlarged state.

source_convention.convention: The 'juan' crop-panel source reports WWII-era European countries on a CONSTANT pre-war/pre-annexation territorial basis rather than adjusting for wartime border changes. Verified independently for Finland (reduced 1940 borders held constant through the 1941-44 Karelia reconquest) and Czechoslovakia (pre-Munich basis held constant through the 1938 partition and 1945 restoration) in 11_retest_conventions.py, and now for Hungary (Trianon+First-Vienna-Award basis held constant through the August 1940 Second Vienna Award and April 1941 Yugoslav occupation, per HUN barley/maize/rye area continuity 1938-1944).
source_convention.evidence: whep_crops_v1.0.parquet HUN item_code 44/56/71 (barley/maize/rye) area 1935-1948 shows no step at 1940; cross-checked against pipelines/polity-autoimprove/11_retest_conventions.py check_juan_finland/check_juan_czechoslovakia which document the same no-step signature for two other countries under this source.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes IIA agricultural data labeled "iran" (1922-1945: cotton, tobacco, tea, raisins, jute, etc.) to IRN-1828-2025. The candidate's wiki page (draft status, but with 10 source citations, mostly to Biger 1995's historical-boundary study) documents Iran's territory as stable from the 1828 Treaty of Turkmenchay through the present, with no territorial changes during the 1922-1945 window: the 1925 Pahlavi succession was a dynastic/regime change only, and the 1941 Anglo-Soviet occupation was a wartime military occupation that did not alter sovereignty or borders (Iran remained a recognized independent state throughout, regaining full control post-war). The 1857 Herat/Afghan-independence adjustment predates the observed span. The staple magnitudes (cotton seed ~58,500 t, cotton lint ~118,000 ha, tobacco ~11,970 ha, tea ~977 ha, raisins ~33,700 t) are all plausible for mainland Iran's agriculture and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change (no sub-territory fold-up, no entrepot signature - these are classic Iranian staples, not goods implausible for its climate/terrain). No neighbor_segments data was available to cross-check, but nothing in the data or the wiki's cited external source suggests the IIA reporting territory differs from national Iran. The wiki page, while unreviewed, rests its territorial-stability claim on an external academic source (Biger 1995) rather than being a bare assertion, which corroborates rather than merely restates the claim.

The assertion routes Mitchell's "Puerto Rico" agricultural series (1850-1960, 173 rows) to PRI-1800-2025 by ISO match. The candidate's wiki page (draft status, but substantive: 8,568 bytes, 12 source citations, no TODOs) makes a well-argued case that Puerto Rico's territorial extent (the island group, ~8,868-8,972 km²) never changed across the whole 1800-2025 span — only its sovereign did, in the 1898 Treaty of Paris cession from Spain to the US. Because Puerto Rico has no land border, no treaty could have moved a frontier; CShapes' own change-detection threshold (100x100km) is an order of magnitude above the island's size, reinforcing that no sub-island partition could have occurred undetected. The staple_magnitudes in the bundle (sugar raw centrifugal median 171,500 t; milk 182,000 t; poultry 850,000 head) are plausible for a single Caribbean island economy of this size and show no sign of a much larger reporting unit (e.g. no Antilles-wide aggregation, no US-mainland-scale figures) or of an entrepot pattern (sugar/coffee/cattle are all genuinely producible on the island, not transshipped). No neighbor_segments exist to check for boundary-vintage effects. The one caveat is that the 1850-1960 span straddles the 1898 sovereignty transfer; while the wiki argues extent was unaffected, that is a sovereignty change during the span, so per the routing rule I mark this best_available rather than verified_equal even though I found no evidence of territorial change.
verdict.wiki_note: Mitchell's 173-row "Puerto Rico" series runs continuously 1850-1960 (109 distinct years) with plausible island-scale magnitudes throughout (sugar raw centrifugal median 171,500t, n=108) and no visible step-change in scale around the 1898 Spain-to-US transfer — weak corroborating evidence toward closing oq-pri-spanish-era-data-basis, though it does not by itself prove the Spanish-era figures used the same territorial basis as the US-era ones.

review.basis: Reconstructing the territory first: Puerto Rico 1850-1960 is an island group with no land frontier — the main island plus Vieques, Culebra and Mona. Across the observed span its extent is constant; the only event is a change of sovereign (Treaty of Paris, 10 Dec 1898, Spain to the United States), which transferred the whole island at once and moved no boundary of extent. The only conceivable in-span accretions (Spanish formalisation of settlement on Vieques in the 1840s-50s and Culebra in 1880) predate or barely touch the span and together are under 2% of ~8,900 km², over territory already under the same claim; there is no annexation, cession, separation or occupation to break the span. So a single 1850-1960 row can equal the reporting territory. Failure-family checks: (1) scope — no union or empire aggregate is at risk; Spanish colonial and later US statistics reported Puerto Rico as its own unit, never as part of a Cuba/Antilles total, and Mitchell's Americas volume carries Cuba and Puerto Rico as separate country entries; (3) combined reporting — no sibling polity shares the label; (5) sub-territory fold-up — "puerto rico" is the whole reporting unit, not a district or municipio, so there is no component-to-parent inflation; (6) entrepot — the staples are agronomically native to the island (cane sugar, green coffee, cattle, goats, horses, milk), not transit goods. Magnitude plausibility settles it: sugar raw centrifugal median 171,500 t over n=108 sits exactly where a continuous island-only series should, given independently sourced figures of under 100,000 tons in 1898 rising past 1,000,000 tons by the late 1930s and peaking in 1952 — the median of that rising 1850-1960 series falls around the 1905-1912 level. Milk 182,000 t and poultry 850,000 head (both short late-span series) are ordinary 1950s figures for an 8,900 km² island of ~2.2 million people, not the numbers of a larger aggregate. The candidate's wiki page is draft but substantive (8.6 KB, 12 citations, no TODOs) and its constant-extent argument matches what I reconstructed independently; I did not rest the verdict on it. Its own open question — whether the pre-1898 Spanish-era rows share the island basis — I could not close from the bundle (no year-by-year series was supplied to test for a step at 1898), but nothing in the magnitudes or in the historical record suggests any other basis existed.

verdict.basis: IIA reports agricultural/mineral commodities under the label 'chile' for 1909-1945, matching the national polity CHL-1902-2025 which spans Chile's modern borders from the post-War-of-the-Pacific settlement onward. The candidate's reviewed wiki page (5 source citations, no TODO markers) documents Chile as a stable national territory over this span, with only a minor boundary rectification with Peru in 1929 (Tacna-Arica treaty, an exchange of small border provinces, not a scope change to the reporting label 'chile' itself — Chile continued to be reported as a single national unit before and after). Staple magnitudes (nitrate/no3 median ~2.45M tonnes, a commodity historically produced almost exclusively in Chile's Atacama desert region acquired in the 1880s; tobacco/beans/fertilizer at plausible national scales) are consistent with national Chilean output and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change across the observed years. No union/empire scope issue (unlike Sweden-Norway or Cisleithania), no combined-reporting risk, and 'Chile' as an ISO/COW national label is not a sub-territory of any larger reporting unit. Because a border adjustment did occur within the 36-year span (1929 Tacna-Arica settlement), per the strict rule for spans over ~30 years this is recorded as best_available rather than verified_equal, even though the change is small and does not materially affect the production data's reporting scope.

Mitchell reports China's mainland and Manchuria as two SEPARATE line items for exactly the same 1932-1944 span: "china mainland|mitchell|1932-1944" (n≈13-25, rice paddy median 32,874,000 t, wheat 12,413,000 t) sits alongside a sibling "china manchuria province of|mitchell|1932-1944" (n=13, rice paddy median 633,000 t, wheat 926,000 t, soybeans 3,785,000 t — routed to MAN-1932-1945). Matching row counts (n=13) and radically different, agronomically-plausible magnitudes (Manchuria's much smaller rice/wheat but larger soybeans/groundnuts, consistent with its cooler climate and soy specialization) show Mitchell itself keeps these two territories distinct throughout the whole span — there is no combined-reporting risk and no double-count between the mainland and Manchukuo labels for this source. Continuity checks against neighboring periods (china mainland 1921-1931 and 1945-1946, both routed to the adjacent CHN sub-periods) show rice-paddy figures in the same 30-33 million order of magnitude before, during, and after 1932-1945, indicating the reporting territory (China proper excluding the three Manchurian provinces) held steady across the split boundaries. The candidate wiki page (draft, 0 source citations) documents this same scope (China proper excl. Manchukuo, composed-difference polygon of CShapes 710 minus Manchukuo provinces) but is internally inconsistent: its "Sourced claims" section cites a rice figure of 812,500 t and its "No split at 1937" Decision cites rice ~46.7M t / wheat ~10.97M t as "national totals" for FAO/IIA "China, mainland" — neither figure matches this bundle's Mitchell-sourced medians (32.87M t rice, 12.41M t wheat), and the Decision text's claim that "china, mainland" 1937-1945 is "geographic all-of-China" data contradicts the page's own Summary/alias table stating the same label denotes China excluding Manchukuo. That internal contradiction is a page-quality finding, not something that undermines this specific Mitchell verdict, which rests on the sibling-label cross-check above rather than on the wiki's narrative. Territory nominally held constant on a "reporting scope" basis, but per policy this 13-year span includes real annexation/occupation events (Manchukuo's 1933 annexation of Rehe, not reflected in the constructed polygon; Japan's 1937-45 occupation of large parts of eastern China) that make the underlying polygon an admitted approximation (~180,000 km2 Rehe drift) rather than an exact match — so confirm_kind is best_available, not verified_equal.
verdict.wiki_note: New corroborating evidence for this Mitchell routing: the assertions ledger's sibling entry "china manchuria province of|mitchell|1932-1944" (routed to MAN-1932-1945) has the same n=13 row count and agronomically distinct magnitudes (rice paddy median 633,000 t, wheat 926,000 t, soybeans 3,785,000 t vs. mainland's 32.87M t rice, 12.41M t wheat) — proof Mitchell itself reports "China, mainland" and Manchuria as separate, non-overlapping territories for the entire 1932-1944 span, ruling out combined-reporting/double-count risk between these two Mitchell labels. Separately, the page's own numbers are internally inconsistent and should be reconciled: the "Sourced claims" section's rice figure of 812,500 t and the "No split at 1937" Decision's rice ~46.7M t/wheat ~10.97M t (attributed to FAO/IIA "China, mainland" and asserted to be "geographic all-of-China," i.e., including Manchukuo) both conflict with each other and with this bundle's Mitchell medians (32.87M t rice, 12.41M t wheat), and the Decision's "all-of-China" framing for 1937-1945 contradicts the page's Summary/alias table, which defines the same label as excluding Manchukuo throughout 1932-1945.

verdict.basis: The assertion routes 171 rows labelled "Cape of Good Hope" (source sa_colonial, 1854-1894) to CAP-1800-1895 (Cape Colony to 1895). "Cape of Good Hope" is not an aggregate or component label — it is a literal historical name for the Cape Colony itself (the colony's own name predates "Cape Province"), and the wiki page documents an existing name_override/applied_alias mapping this exact string to CAP dating from WU-02 (2026-06-23). The page is draft status but unusually well-evidenced for the territorial-scope question: it quantifies the CShapes 1886 polygon vintage-drift (600,802 km², overstating pre-1880 extent by ~85,000 km²/14% due to the Griqualand West annexation), documents that it tested and rejected an alternative Cliopatria series as measuring a different object (British sphere of control including Transvaal, excluding Griqualand West), and explicitly states the Cape's territory did NOT stay constant across 1852-1894 (Griqualand West 1880, Transkeian territories 1885-1894 both fall inside the observed span). Staple magnitudes (wheat ~2.7M bushels, barley ~820k, oast ~1.37M) are plausible in scale for a colonial agricultural returns series and show no entrepot/re-export red flags. Given the span 1854-1894 includes two documented territorial expansions, and CShapes offers only a single 1886 vintage for the whole 1800-1895 row, the routing is the best available match but cannot be verified_equal — the reporting territory changed mid-span. This mirrors the reasoning the page already worked through for the related "south africa" label (1852-1894 portion), which used the identical CAP-1800-1895 routing and was previously banked best_available for the same reason.

The assertion routes FAO/Juan crop-panel rows labeled "ecuador" (ISO=ecu), 1900-1941, to ECU-1800-1942 via ISO match. Ecuador is a whole sovereign national polity, not a component of any larger union (no fold-up/union-scope issue), and there is no combined-reporting risk (no other territory sharing this label). Staple magnitudes (cocoa ~25,500t, coffee ~6,100t, rice ~34,450t, rubber ~1,262t) are plausible for national Ecuador in this era, consistent with its well-documented early-20th-century cacao-export economy — no agronomic-impossibility (entrepot) red flags. The wiki page (draft, thin: 2020 bytes, 1 source citation) is the only existing candidate for the full 1800-1942 span and there is no finer-grained existing Ecuador polity in the database to reroute or split to. However, the observed 42-year span is not territorially constant: web research confirms Ecuador ceded roughly 180,000 km2 to Colombia via the Muñoz Vernaza-Suárez Treaty (1916), and its border with Peru remained an actively disputed/shifting frontier until the 1941 war and the January 1942 Rio Protocol (which the page does note, but only as the end-of-row event, not as evidence the pre-1942 territory itself was unstable). Since the reporting territory changed mid-span via a real cession, per the routing rules this must be recorded as best_available even though ECU-1800-1942 remains the best (only) existing match for the whole 1900-1941 window.
verdict.wiki_note: The observed span (1900-1941) was not territorially constant: Ecuador ceded ~180,000 km2 in the northeast (Putumayo/Napo/Caquetá basins) to Colombia via the Muñoz Vernaza-Suárez Treaty of 1916/1917, and the Ecuador-Peru frontier remained an actively contested, unstable line throughout this period until the 1941 war and the January 1942 Rio Protocol. The page currently only documents the 1942 end-of-row event; it does not mention the 1916 Colombia cession, which means the "1800-1942" row's territory shrank mid-span independent of the 1942 split. No finer-grained existing Ecuador polity captures the pre/post-1916 distinction, so ECU-1800-1942 remains the best available match, but it should not be treated as a fixed, constant territory across the full span.

review.basis: Numbers first: I pulled the full juan/ecu series from state/matched_rows.parquet rather than relying on the medians. Cocoa runs 19-31 kt in 1900-09, rises to a peak of 47.2 kt in 1915 and 44.7 kt in 1920, then collapses to 10.6 kt by 1933 — this is the signature national trajectory of Ecuador as the world's leading cacao exporter before WWI and its post-1920 witches'-broom/monilia collapse, at a level no single province or district could carry and far below any supra-national aggregate. Coffee (2.4 kt in the 1900s, 14 kt by 1935) and rice paddy (16 kt in 1916, 39 kt mid-1930s, 92 kt in 1941) are likewise whole-country coastal-Guayas magnitudes. No union/empire scope issue exists for Ecuador, no colonial fold-up, no entrepot signature (the commodities are exactly what the Costa grows). Continuity across our 1942 period split is smooth in every staple: cocoa 14,400 (1941) -> 13,800 (1942), coffee 14,600 -> 11,800, rice 91,700 -> 122,900 (a genuine wartime boom that continues through 1947, not a level step). That is decisive: the reporting territory did not change at the Rio de Janeiro Protocol, because the ceded Amazonian territory produced nothing that entered these statistics. So the label's reporting basis is effective-control agricultural Ecuador — Costa plus Sierra — invariant across 1900-1960, whereas the candidate polity is defined by the pre-1942 CLAIMED extent (CShapes cowcode=130 at 1886 vintage) and exists as a separate row precisely because of a territorial change the data never registers. The candidate is the right and only row for these years, but reporting territory does not equal the polity's mapped territory and the polity's claimed extent was itself not constant over 1900-1941 (Peruvian advance, 1922 Salomon-Lozano, 1941 war), hence best_available rather than verified_equal. The wiki page is a 2,020-byte CSV-derived stub whose sole citation is the database itself; it contributed nothing beyond the date of the Rio Protocol and I did not rest the verdict on it.
review.wiki_note: Production data (juan series) show no discontinuity at the 1942 Rio Protocol split: cocoa 14.4 kt (1941) -> 13.8 kt (1942), coffee 14.6 -> 11.8 kt, rice paddy continuing its wartime rise. The Amazonian territory lost in 1942 contributed nothing to recorded agricultural output, so the ECU-1800-1942 / ECU-1942-2025 split is politically real but statistically inert — series may be joined across it without a scope adjustment. Correspondingly, agricultural statistics for this row are on effective-control Ecuador (Costa + Sierra), not on the wider claimed extent that the 1886-vintage CShapes polygon depicts; the page has no area figure and no territorial description of its own.

verdict.basis: The IIA 'guatemala' label for 1910-1945 reports on the national territory of the Republic of Guatemala, which had been stable since separation from the United Provinces of Central America in the late 1830s; no annexation, cession, or union-scope ambiguity affects this republic during 1910-1945 (unlike Sweden-Norway or Austria-Hungary style cases). The reported staple magnitudes (cacao ~656 t median, cotton lint ~117 ha, tobacco ~180 t, groundnuts ~14 ha) are modest smallholder-agriculture figures fully consistent with Guatemala's known small-scale tropical agricultural profile in this era and show no discontinuity suggesting a scope change. There is no entrepot/re-export concern (Guatemala is not a transit hub for these commodities) and no combined-reporting risk (Guatemala was never merged with a neighboring polity in official statistics during this span). The wiki page, though draft-status, documents the country's stable post-1830s boundary, and I corroborate this independently via well-established historical-geography knowledge of Central American state formation rather than relying on the page's assertions alone.

The assertion routes whep_crops "chile" agricultural data (barley, beans, maize, chick peas, peas — central-valley staple crops) for 1860-1883 to CHL-1810-1884 ("Chile to 1884"), the pre-War-of-the-Pacific polity bounded at 24°S. The candidate's wiki page (draft status, but unusually deep and well-cited for a draft — treaty dates, measured polygon arithmetic, explicit decision log) documents that the 24°S Chile-Bolivia border was fixed by the 1866 Treaty of Mutual Benefits and reaffirmed 1874, that everything Chile gained in the War of the Pacific (Tarapacá, the Bolivian Litoral/Antofagasta) lies north of that line, and that the transfer only completed via the Treaty of Ancón (Oct 1883) and Truce of Valparaíso (1884) — which is exactly why the page's own end_year was corrected from 1883 to 1884 to keep 1883 inside this polity rather than the post-war successor. The crops in this assertion (barley, beans, maize, peas, chickpeas) are central-Chile agricultural staples, not products of the Atacama desert/nitrate provinces that changed hands, so the reporting territory for this commodity basket was materially unaffected by the war and stayed within core pre-annexation Chile for the entire 1860-1883 span. The northern boundary is described on the page as "exact, on the treaty parallel" from 1866 onward (and only loosely defined 1860-1865, before formalization); the page's only acknowledged imprecision (polygon_status=proxy) concerns the eastern Patagonian claim line, which is irrelevant to agricultural crop reporting. Given the minor pre-1866 border ambiguity and the general proxy/constructed nature of the polygon, I classify this as best_available rather than verified_equal, though the match is strong.

The observed span (1947-1951) falls entirely after the 10 Feb 1947 Paris Peace Treaty, which confirmed the post-1940 Moscow Treaty losses (Karelia, Salla) plus the additional cession of Petsamo. Finland's territory was stable and unchanged for the whole 1947-1951 window (no annexations/cessions occurred within that span; the only fluctuation -- Continuation War 1941-1944 briefly regaining then re-losing Karelia -- predates the observed years and is irrelevant here). This matches candidate FIN-1940-2025's documented territory (~338,000 km2, post-1940/1947 borders) exactly, and that territory persisted unchanged through 1951 and indeed to the present, so it is both equal and constant across the whole observed span. Staple magnitudes (rye ~176k ha, meat ~58k t) are plausible for Finland's post-war reduced territory and population, with no sign of a truncated or expanded reporting basis. The wiki page (draft status, 7 source citations from biger-1995) documents the territorial history accurately and its own open question (oq-continuation-war-territory) is already scoped to 1941-1944, which is outside our 1947-1951 span, so it does not undermine this verdict.

The candidate THA-1909-2025 is a reviewed wiki page with 4 source citations (Biger 1995) documenting stable borders from the 1909 Anglo-Siamese Treaty (cession of the Malay states) through the present, with only minor WWII-era occupations (Shan/Malay/Cambodian territories, ~1941-1945) that were reverted post-war and thus did not constitute a lasting change in the reporting territory. The observed span 1911-1944 falls almost entirely within the stable pre-WWII border period. The IIA data items (cotton lint, cotton seed, rubber, sesame seed, tobacco) with magnitudes in the thousands of hectares (rubber median ~163,450 ha reflecting the South Thailand rubber belt) are all agronomically plausible for mainland Thailand and show no signs of a scope discontinuity. No entrepot/re-export or sub-territory fold-up concerns apply -- 'Thailand'/'Siam' as an IIA reporting label is a national aggregate matching the whole kingdom, not a component.

review.basis: The label under IIA is "siam" (Siam renamed Thailand 1939), and the source's own stated areas settle the scope question decisively: data/final/source_stated_areas.csv gives IIA's declared area for SIAM as 484,128 km² (1909 yearbook, both 1911 and 1921 reference years), 518,159 km² (1925 yearbook), 518,376 km² (1929/1932/1933) and 513,450 km² (1938) — all within ~1% of the candidate's documented ~513,120 km² except the early 1909 survey figure, which is 5.7% low and is a measurement vintage artefact, not a different territory. So the reporting unit is Siam proper, on post-1909 Anglo-Siamese-Treaty borders, exactly the candidate's basis. iia_label_provenance.csv records the label as one_to_one, no parent label, zero sub-labels, no mixing observed, dominant raw label "siam" at 100% — ruling out both combined reporting and sub-territory fold-up. Staple magnitudes are agronomically coherent for Siam and show no entrepot signature: rubber ~163,450 ha (peninsular south, consistent with late-1930s Siamese plantings), tobacco ~9.9k ha, cotton lint ~4k ha, sesame ~1k ha — small industrial/oilseed acreages against a rice economy, nothing that overshoots the territory. No neighbour segments exist because THA-1909-2025 is not split within the observed window, so no magnitude step is available or expected. I withhold verified_equal for one reason: the observed span runs to 1944, and Thailand's actual territory was NOT constant across 1911-1944 — the 1941 Franco-Thai settlement (Battambang/Siem Reap/Champasak), the 1942 Shan state occupation and the 1943 Japanese transfer of Kedah, Perlis, Kelantan and Terengganu all enlarged it before the 1946 reversion. The candidate polygon is fixed 1909 borders, and I could not establish from the source whether the handful of 1941-44 IIA/successor figures were compiled on wartime or pre-war extent; either way no single constant-territory polity can equal the reporting territory over the whole span, so best_available is the honest kind.
review.wiki_note: IIA's own stated areas for SIAM corroborate the page's ~513,120 km²: 518,376 km² (1929-1933 yearbooks) and 513,450 km² (1938), with an earlier 484,128 km² in the 1909 yearbook that reflects survey vintage rather than a different territory. Note also that IIA-sourced rows for Thailand extend to 1944, i.e. into the 1941-45 wartime annexations (Battambang/Siem Reap, Shan states, and the four Malay states returned by Japan in 1943) which the fixed 1909 polygon does not cover; the compilation basis of those final years is unresolved.

verdict.basis: The assertion covers "Madagascar" in FAO 1952 yearbook data for years 1939-1951. Madagascar is an island nation with no land boundaries, so there is no union/empire-scope ambiguity (unlike Sweden-Norway or Austria-Hungary) and no sub-territory fold-up risk (no smaller labeled component here). The candidate MDG-1882-2025 covers the whole island from French involvement (1882) through independence (1960) to present; per the wiki's own sub-chain notes, the French colony reached its full/expanded territorial extent by 1912 and held constant through 1946 (overseas territory) and beyond — the observed span 1939-1951 falls entirely within this constant-territory window (full island under French colonial administration), well before independence in 1960. The 1939-1951 FAO figures (rice paddy ~636k ha, tobacco ~5k ha, sweet potatoes ~182k ha, poultry ~400k heads) are plausible in scale for the whole island of Madagascar, not a sub-region, and there is no entrepot/re-export concern (Madagascar is agriculturally self-producing for these staples, not a transit hub). The wiki page (draft, 2 citations) is thin but its core territorial claim — island of Madagascar, no land boundaries, colonial administration expanded to cover the whole island by 1912 — is independently corroborated by well-established geography/history (Madagascar's colonial borders were fixed by the early 1910s and unchanged through the FAO reporting period). No annexation, cession, or partition occurred during 1939-1951 itself, so the reporting territory was constant across the whole observed span and equals the candidate's territory.

Montserrat is a single small (100.6 km²) island BOT that has been a continuous, undivided British colonial administrative unit since the 17th century, with no annexation/cession/partition events during the observed 1909-1945 span. The IIA staple magnitudes (cotton lint ~554 ha, cotton seed ~871 ha, lemons/limes ~500 t, raw sugar ~100 t) are all plausible for a ~100 km² Caribbean island economy — cotton and lime/citrus production were in fact historically documented Montserrat export staples in this era, which independently corroborates that the "Montserrat" label in IIA is reporting the island itself rather than a broader federation aggregate or an entrepot re-export figure. There is no sub-territory fold-up risk (the label IS the smallest administrative unit, not a component folded into a parent) and no union/empire-scope ambiguity (Montserrat, unlike some Leeward Islands reporting, appears to be itemized separately by IIA under its own name). Since the island's physical/administrative extent did not change across 1909-1945, this is a verified_equal confirm, not merely best_available.

FAO 1952 Yearbook follows standard FAO practice of reporting metropolitan Portugal separately from its African/Atlantic colonies (Angola, Mozambique, Cape Verde, etc. appear as their own line items in this source, not folded into 'Portugal'), so the label's reporting territory is metropolitan Portugal, matching candidate PRT-1800-2025 which per its own wiki page is explicitly the metropolitan-only continuous row (colonies tracked as separate WHEP rows, no split for 1822 Brazil or 1974-75 African decolonization since metropolitan borders didn't move). The staple magnitudes (oats 188k ha, grapes 360k ha, meat 31k t) are plausible for metropolitan Portugal's ~92,000 km2 and are consistent in scale across the 1934-1951 span with no jump suggesting a scope change; Portugal's metropolitan borders with Spain were unchanged throughout this span (stable since 1297, reconfirmed 1815), and no annexation/cession/occupation affected metropolitan Portugal 1934-1951 (Iberian neutrality in WWII). The population figure (median 1,419k) looked anomalously low for Portugal's ~8M population, but the bundle's own source_conventions entry already resolved this: fao1952's population item code mixes five distinct indicators (total, agricultural, agricultural-occupied, male/female splits) under one code, and the low median reflects a sub-indicator, not a territorial mismatch -- this is prior-established knowledge, not new information from this check.

The assertion routes FAO 1952 Syrian agricultural/livestock data (years 1949-1951, 162 rows) to SYR-1946-1967. This observed span falls entirely within the stable interior of the candidate's territorial period: Syria gained independence 17 April 1946 (French mandate evacuation) and its territory (~185,701 km² per CShapes, including the Golan Heights) remained constant until the tiny Golan reduction on 1967-06-10 and was unaffected by the 1958-1961 UAR merger gap (that occurs 7-10 years after the observed span, well outside 1949-1951). So neither of the two known discontinuities in this polity's life (UAR 1958, Golan 1967) touches the 1949-1951 window — the reporting territory is unambiguously post-mandate independent Syria for the whole observed span. Staple magnitudes (poultry ~70k head, meat ~20k tonnes, cotton lint on ~42k ha, dry beans ~2k ha) are plausible in scale for mid-century Syria and show no sign of a narrower sub-territory or a broader Levant aggregate. The neighbor segment for 1937-1939 correctly routes to the mandate-era predecessor SYR-1922-1946, confirming continuity of reporting territory across the mandate/independence transition (no scope change accompanied independence). The source_conventions entry about FAO1952's five population indicators is not relevant to this label's items (agricultural production/livestock, not population) and does not bear on territorial scope. The wiki page (draft status, treated as hypothesis) documents the same history (independence date, constant CShapes area 1946-1967 except the 1967 Golan step, UAR gap 1958-1961) — this corroborates but the underlying facts (Syrian independence 1946, Golan loss 1967, UAR 1958-1961) are well-established historical facts independent of this specific draft page, so the conclusion is not circular. No sub-territory fold-up, entrepot, or combined-reporting concern applies to a country-level FAO agricultural table for Syria in this era.

review.basis: Territory first: Syria's borders were static across the whole observed span 1949-1951. The Sanjak of Alexandretta/Hatay was ceded to Turkey in 1939 (before the span); Latakia and Jabal Druze were reintegrated into the Syrian state by 1942-46; independence came 17 April 1946 with French evacuation; the next territorial change is the Golan in June 1967. The 1949-51 coups (Zaim, Hinnawi, Shishakli) and the March 1950 rupture of the Syrian-Lebanese customs union were regime/fiscal events, not territorial ones — a customs union is not a territory. So one polity, SYR-1946-1967, can equal the reporting territory for the entire span. On the source side I checked the two live failure families directly in the FAO 1952 extraction (/home/usuario/Nextcloud/whep/layer_b/consolidated_layer_b.parquet, 23,801 fao1952 rows): (a) combined Syria+Lebanon reporting — the yearbook carries THREE distinct labels, "Syria" (200 rows, 48 items), "Lebanon" (145 rows, 45 items) and "Syria and Lebanon" (8 rows, tobacco only, already routed to the separate aggregate SYL-1944-1953). Lebanon is reported separately for the same years 1949-51, so the "Syria" label is Syria proper, and the joint label is confined to tobacco; (b) magnitude plausibility — the label's own total-population row is 3,579k for 1951, matching accepted Syria-alone figures (~3.4-3.5M) and clearly excluding Lebanon (~1.3M); the cotton series is the decisive tell, area 25 -> 78 -> 217 thousand ha and lint 13 -> 35 -> 49 thousand tonnes over 1949-51, which is exactly the documented Jazira cotton boom of Syria proper (Lebanon's own cotton rows are 1-5 thousand ha), impossible under any broader or narrower scope. No sub-territory fold-up (the label is a state, not a province), no entrepot issue, no vintage lag (the figures move year to year with real Syrian events rather than repeating a pre-war base). The candidate's wiki page is draft but its territorial account (185,701 km2, stable until 1967-06-10) is consistent with what I reconstructed independently; I did not lean on it for the routing decision.

verdict.basis: The assertion is FAO 1952 "India" data for 1949-1951 (161 rows, various commodities/livestock: camels, sugar, chick peas, coffee, cotton, groundnuts, tobacco, horses/mules/asses). Candidate IND-1949-2025 is the Republic of India from independence-era borders onward. Although the wiki page is nominally "draft," it is unusually well-corroborated (3 source citations, detailed CShapes/GADM cross-checks) and documents that the Goa (1961) and Sikkim (1975) territorial changes are the only ones affecting this row, both well after the observed 1949-1951 span — so for this specific span India's territory is exactly the Republic of India at independence, matching the source label with no union/empire, sub-territory, or entrepot ambiguity. Staple magnitudes (millions of hectares for cotton/groundnuts, hundreds of thousands of head for horses/mules/asses) are plausible at India's national scale, not a fraction-of-country size that would suggest fold-up. Neighbor segments show continuous IND-* period chaining (1937-1940 -> 1948 -> 1949-1951) with no discontinuity implying a scope change. Source_conventions note (population-series indicator mixing) does not bear on this production/livestock-heavy assertion. No annexation/cession affects territory within 1949-1951 itself, so the reporting territory is both equal to the candidate's and constant across the whole observed span, supporting verified_equal.

Assertion routes IIA "kenya" commodity data (161 rows, 1930-1945, ISO=ken) to KEN-1926-1963 (Kenya Colony, 1926 Rudolf-province transfer to 1963 independence) via iso+prior routing. The candidate's territory (Kenya Colony under CShapes/Biger, ~582,646 km², bounded by Sudan/South Sudan, Ethiopia, Somalia, Indian Ocean, Tanzania, Uganda) was stable across the entire 1926-1963 period — no annexations, cessions, or administrative splits affecting Kenya's boundaries occurred between 1926 and 1963 (the only 20th-century boundary change, the 1925 Jubaland cession to Italy, predates this polity's 1926 start and the neighboring segment KEN-1907-1924 already accounts for the pre-1926 phase). The observed span 1930-1945 falls entirely within this stable period, well clear of the 1926 start-boundary. Staple magnitudes (tea ~5,000 ha, coffee ~39,000 ha, cotton lint ~1,162 t) are all plausible for a territory this size and are the kind of smallholder/settler-estate crops historically reported for colonial Kenya — no discontinuity or entrepot/agronomic-impossibility signal. The label "kenya" is a straightforward national-scale label with no sub-territory fold-up risk (it is not a province or component name). The wiki page, though marked draft, is reasonably substantive (2816 bytes, 7 source citations from Biger 1995 and CShapes) and its territorial claims (colonial Kenya boundaries, 1926 Rudolf Province transfer, 1963 independence) are externally corroborated (Biger 1995 boundary history, matches standard historical-geography accounts of Kenya Colony) rather than resting solely on the page's own assertion. No contradiction or error found in the page. Verdict: confirm, verified_equal — territory equals the candidate's and was constant across the whole 1930-1945 span.

Barbados is a single 430 km2 island, continuously British from 1627 to 1966, with no land boundary and no documented territorial change of any kind; the observed span (1850-1960) falls entirely within that unbroken colonial tenure, well before the 1966 independence (a sovereignty change, not a territorial one) and mostly before the 1958-1962 West Indies Federation (only 1958-1960 overlaps, and the Federation was a political union of separate territories, not a merger, so Barbados' own land area did not change). The staple magnitudes (sugar cane ~15,000 ha median on a ~43,000 ha island, raw sugar ~52,500 tonnes median) are internally consistent with Barbados' well-documented history as an intensely sugar-monocultured small island and show no sign of entrepot re-export or scope inflation. No annexation, cession, or boundary change occurred anywhere inside 1850-1960, so the reporting territory equals the candidate's and was constant across the whole span - a legitimate verified_equal case despite the 110-year length, because Barbados genuinely never split.
